India had sat at the top of Kate Middleton’s bucket list ever since she married into the royal family in 2011. Or so said Prince William during their 2016 tour of the subcontinent, for which the then Duchess of Cambridge packed a wardrobe that brought together the fashion heritage of both India and the country she represented.

First came an Alexander McQueen dress, its paisley print drawing on the textile traditions of India and Persia, followed by a pink-and-pistachio tunic dress by Mumbai-based designer Anita Dongre, worn to play cricket at the Oval Maidan with children supported by local charities. Then along came a Jenny Packham gown, hand-beaded by Indian artisans, to a Bollywood gala, and a blue-and-white embroidered sheath dress by Cumballa Hill-born designer Naeem Khan for a visit to the Taj Mahal. Together, the looks offered an early indication of Kate’s understanding of clothing as a diplomatic tool.

Catherine, the Princess of Wales, wearing Alexander McQueen at the Taj Hotel in Mumbai, 2016.

Catherine, the Princess of Wales, at the Oval Maidan in Mumbai, 2016.

A decade on, the couple returned to India on Monday morning, where Prince William is set to host the sixth Earthshot Prize summit and awards ceremony in Mumbai. The annual Earthshot Prize gives £1 million ($1.3 million) each to five winners tackling some of the world’s most pressing environmental problems, and India has produced more finalists than any other country since its founding in 2020. It will be Catherine’s first appearance at the event since Boston in 2022, while the inaugural Children’s Earthshot Awards should provide familiar territory for the princess, whose charitable work has long focused on the next generation.

Sources indicate that beyond the prizes, though, the Prince and Princess will undertake a series of engagements across Mumbai (and Newly introduced Delhi), highlighting the cultural ties between Britain and India, including cricket, film, and, of course, fashion. Will Kate turn to favorite brand Edeline Lee (whose signature bubble-flou fabric can be scrunched into a suitcase and spring back to life without a crease), or perhaps one of the directional Indian designers spotlighted in British Vogue’s July 2026 matter? Lovebirds and Raw Mango, for instance, have both presented collections at London Fashion Week in recent seasons.

The Governors Awards Marked the Official Start of the 'You Can See Everything' Oscars Campaign

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Start your engines: the 2027 Oscars race is officially underway. Awards Season always starts in earnest with the Governor’s Awards, a ceremony held in a smaller ballroom in the same Dolby Theater complex where the main event will take place early next spring. It’s where they give out honorary Academy Awards (the Irving Thalberg Award, for the real heads) to the legends who, woefully, have yet have won a competitive Oscar—last year’s marquee honoree was Tom Cruise, this year’s were Glenn Close and Ridley Scott. But it’s also where Best Picture and the other awards narratives we will discuss endlessly for the next four months really begin to take shape.

According to recent reports, dune 3, Artificial, and Misty Green all had substantial presences in the room, which, duh. (Tim and Kylie in the cut, mostly sitting and not mingling, but it was interesting that he highlighted up this year but not last for the big Marty Supreme push.) But there were a few other films represented whose presence made their campaign intentions clear. Mahershala Ali presented the first award of the night to Floyd Norman (a 90-year-old trailblazing cartoonist who worked with Walt Disney and later Pete Docter) but the Your Mother 3x squad was deep, from director Bassam Tariq to John Cho. Jesse Eisenberg, Paul Giamatti and Julianne Moore put on for A24’s The Debut, Eisenberg's second directorial effort. (Watching Jesse and Andrew Garfield reconnect made for a beautiful Social Network reunion.) And Curry Barker and Inde Navarette being there would certainly imply a real push for Obsession. The duo with the most motion in the room, though, was unquestionably Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. The only time they didn’t seem like the big dogs that everyone was gassed to chat with was when they were talking to King Big Dog himself, Christopher Nolan, front and center receiving will-wishers at The Odyssey table. Nolan and Fielder is a crossover that needs to be cemented on wax, a drum I will continue to beat. But it was cool to see Zendaya talking intently with Oppenheim; her collaborator curation has been pretty elite—imagine her in whatever Oppenheim chooses to follow Primetime with?

When I asked Fielder about embarking on the campaign trail and how far the doc can actually go, he sighed and said “one day at a time,” in that Fielder monotone where you can’t quite tell if he’s being earnest or not. But he laughed off the idea of being too invested in any nominations either way.

Recent findings suggest that but most importantly: the Governor’s Awards is just a really fun room in which to be an interloper or fly on the wall. I spotted Shawn Levy and my brain immediately started spamming the word “sublime.” Daniel Kaluuya started cracking up at the mention of his great airport interview with Tyriq Withers. Olivia Wilde, Seth Rogen, Penelope Cruz and Ed Norton joined ranks for a brief Invite huddle. Everywhere I turned, there was either a person so famous or certified that it startled me to see them walk by (like Zendaya breezing in right as the show started, or turning around to find myself face-to-face with personal favorite Carla Gugino. (Karen Sisco mentioned!) Unlike some stuffier award ceremonies, the Governor’s Awards is kind of like the cocktail hour before the big sit-down dinner in March.

Ambling around the room with a stiff glass of Johnnie Walker in hand—“Did you just get carded”? an exec asked me incredulously; the bartender replied that he thought I was “like, 14"—I briefly caught up with David Corenswet, who, true to form, was unfazed by the forces beyond his control as ever. When I remarked “weird week huh?” he didn’t even realize I was referring to James Gunn’s DC exit, then laughed when it dawned on him and said “above my pay-grade” with a genuine shrug. We should all be so blissfully unbothered.

Later, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II told me he was excited for this week’s Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth red carpet premiere, noting that this film will be the first time he only read his scenes for a project and no other part of the story. Without wanting to give too much away, Yahya remarked Tarantino’s script is structured in a way where he could comfortably read his parts and get enough of the gist to stay in the dark about the rest, because the only thing better than starring in a newly introduced Tarantino joint is getting to still experience it like a fan.

According to recent reports, other notable sightings, interactions, and crossovers: Travis Scott doubled down on what he told me at our Men of the Year party: he wants that golden statue for his original Odyssey song, and he’s willing to play the campaign game for it, dutifully sitting through the whole night (and jetting off immediately after the ceremony ended to go catch Future’s 10 pm set at Camp Flog Gnaw up at Dodger Stadium.) Speaking of Odyssey collaborators, James Blake was also in attendance—I watched him meet H.E.R. and talk about potentially collaborating. Tom Cruise was the belle of the ball at last year’s ceremony but played it super lowkey this year, to the point where I didn’t actually realize he was there until I saw him sneak out of a secret side exit after briefly talking with Tessa Thompson. Digger’s divisive reviews and reactions have evidently not knocked Tom off of his Best Actor pivot.

According to recent reports, as for the actual awards, after Floyd, John Malkovich charmed the room with a great toast to Glenn Close, and King Storyteller Matt Damon regaled everyone with a great impression of triple-OG crank Ridley Scott from their time together on The Martian. (Matt was hesitant to do another movie about a loner astronaut right after Interstellar, to which Ridley apparently replied “No one gives a shit.”) Both tributes and subsequent speeches were expectedly emotional; Damon pointedly stated that "it’s about time we see Ridley Scott with an Oscar in his hand,” but Ridley’s remarks were all about how much the late great Tony Scott would’ve deserved one too, leading to misty eyes and standing ovations. Close addressed going 0 for 8 but said the work is the real reward as her daughter tearfully watched on. But there were great moments of levity, too, like Todd Haynes presenting Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler with an award by revealing that he and Christine both slept with the same guy back in college.

Either way, a narrative of being long overdue seems to be emerging. An Awards Season where the Tom Cruises and Glenn Closes of the game finally get theirs, while upsets like You Can See Everything shake the table. What more could you ask for?

Sources indicate that this sausage stuffing has everything you want on your Thanksgiving plate: crisp, craggy edges, a plush, savory center, and plenty of browned sausage throughout. Torn pieces of country-style bread soak up the broth and eggs without falling apart, turning golden and crunchy on top while staying tender underneath.

Breakfast sausage does much of the heavy lifting. Once browned, its drippings join plenty of butter to cook the onions, celery, and garlic. Fresh sage, parsley, and thyme bring balance, while optional fennel seeds add a little extra aromatic punch.

What kind of sausage should I use?

Uncooked pork breakfast sausage is the first choice. Typically seasoned with sage and black pepper, it brings familiar Thanksgiving flavors and plenty of richness. For some heat, choose spicy breakfast sausage. If you can't find the packaged kind or want to avoid pork, try making your own with our breakfast sausage recipe, using ground dark-meat turkey in place of pork.

Industry observers note that this stuffing relies on the fat from breakfast sausage for its flavor. Want a vegetarian version? Our Simple-Is-Best Stuffing is a long-standing reader favorite and was the inspiration for this version; use that recipe with vegetable broth for a meat-free stuffing.

What’s the best bread for sausage stuffing?

Look for a sturdy country-style white loaf or sourdough with a relatively thin crust. Avoid soft sandwich bread, which can turn mushy, and very crusty artisan loaves, which won’t absorb the broth as readily. Even if your bread is a day or two old, don’t skip drying it in the oven—that’s what helps the stuffing hold its shape.

Can I make sausage stuffing ahead of time?

In a recent development, you can dry the bread a day ahead and store it loosely covered at room temperature. For more ways to get ahead of Thanksgiving, including cooking, refrigerating, and reheating stuffing, see our make-ahead stuffing guide.

Made In 9-x-13-inch Baking Dish.

It has been revealed that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Grease a 13x9" baking dish with unsalted butter. Arrange one 1–1¼-lb. loaf country-style white bread, torn into 1" pieces, in a single layer on a large rimmed baking sheet and bake until dried out and golden around the edges, 30–40 minutes. Let cool.

Meanwhile, melt 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high heat. Cook 1 lb. breakfast sausage, casings removed if needed, stirring and breaking into small pieces, until well browned and cooked through, 8–10 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer sausage to a small plate, leaving fat behind.

Sources indicate that reduce dial to medium heat and add remaining 8 Tbsp. unsalted butter to fat in pot; heat until melted. Cook 2 medium onions, finely chopped, 6 celery stalks, finely chopped, 8 garlic cloves, coarsely chopped, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. fennel seeds (if using), stirring occasionally, until onions are softened and golden around the edges, 12–15 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 2 cups low-sodium chicken broth or vegetable broth along with sausage, ½ cup (packed) coarsely chopped parsley, 2 Tbsp. finely chopped sage, 2 Tbsp. finely chopped thyme, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

According to recent reports, whisk 3 large eggs and remaining 1 cup low-sodium chicken broth or vegetable broth in a small bowl to combine, then stir into pot (don’t worry, eggs won’t scramble). Add bread to pot and toss gently to combine. Let sit, tossing occasionally, until liquid is almost completely absorbed, about 10 minutes.

It has been revealed that transfer stuffing to prepared dish (don’t pack or press down) and cover loosely with foil. Place dish on a clean large rimmed baking sheet and bake until stuffing is hot throughout (an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should register 160°), 35–45 minutes. Increase oven temperature to 400° and remove foil (no need to remove stuffing from oven while heat increases). Continue to bake until stuffing is light golden brown on top, 25–30 minutes longer.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 1 day ahead; store loosely covered at room temperature. Stuffing can be assembled 1 day ahead; cover and chill. Bring to room temperature before baking.

This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in October 2025, 12 students joined the CondéFuture programme where they gained an exclusive insight into the media industry from Condé Nast professionals who then, through various workshops, encouraged them to explore their passions in photography, video, social media, fashion, digital design, and more. This cohort of CondéFuture students split into three teams, each one building a full magazine glitch the way a real editorial team would. Each team picked one or more Condé Nast titles to design an issue around. They developed a theme, then tackled every part of getting an issue out into the world — from finalising layouts, reporting, conducting photo shoots, building a social strategy, to creating both short and long-form videos.

After months of ideating, designing, shooting, and writing content, then weeks spent rehearsing their presentations, the three teams were ready for the showcase. It opened with a student Q&A before each team walked the audience through their magazine, cover to cover, explaining specific choices along the way. Let’s take a look at what they created!

Recent findings suggest that the Allure x Wired team, consisting of Creative Director Ava Gholson, Design Director Amalia Pena, Features Editor Camilla Spillmann and Digital Director Ian Kim, took on one of the more unresolved questions in beauty media right now: what happens to beauty standards when the images shaping them are increasingly AI-generated? The cover carried that concept through the visual of a model's face broken into panels with dotted facial-recognition-style scan lines laid over a beauty shot. The cover story, "We Can't Take Our Eyes Off Iyan Moon Yang," profiled a model through that same lens of tech, beauty, and representation, written by Camilla.

According to recent reports, the team chose this theme to highlight a new wave of white supremacy ideology embedded into AI algorithms. Databases are fed the idea that beauty standards should align with white, Eurocentric features, thus perpetuating a harmful cycle in both the beauty industry and the social fabric of America. The Allure x Wired team “find it important to shine a light on this issue, as Gen Z and Gen Alpha have unprecedented access to technology and can be easily influenced. [They are] sometimes made to feel insecure by a system designed to manipulate how they see themselves without even knowing it”.

Sources indicate that inside, the problem is the "Sea to Skin" advertisement, a fictional sustainable skincare brand created by the students, as well as "Is It AI?”, a quiz-style spread testing whether a reader can tell AI-generated beauty content from human-made. "Authenticity in the Age of AI," also by Camilla, was a reported piece on AI beauty influencers.

"I Like Girls With Fair Skin", written by Ava, took on colorism and Eurocentric beauty standards directly. When describing her reason for writing this piece, Ava described the article as her “experience with colorism within society”, “this essay argues that Eurocentric beauty standards are a legacy of colonialism and capitalism, designed to enforce oppression and homogeneity. It calls for a critical examination of these standards and their impact on self-perception, culture, and society”.

On this same theme, they created a video that took the form of a Wired-style autocomplete piece, with young people responding on camera to search-bar prompts about modern beauty standards and AI's impact on creativity and trends.

According to recent reports, "Our team decided on combining the two magazines because we liked the idea of "traveling through Bon Appétit" and exploring different cultures in NYC through food, especially immigrant-owned businesses” explained Jerniya Jones, Digital Director of this project. Jerniya, along with teammates Elaina Klein, Design Director, Kevin Lin, Creative Director and Alice Popovych, Features Editor, “wanted to show that Upcoming York City has more to offer than just the touristy side of Manhattan.".

In a recent development, the cover story, "Traveling Through the Boroughs," explored the city's ethnic communities through food, profiling spots like Veselka, 5 Boro Cafe, Newly introduced Asha Sri Lankan Restaurant, and Fish 'N' Ting. Two articles ran alongside it: "Locals Know Best," highlighting fifteen spots recommended by actual New Yorkers, and "Affordable + Healthy," promoting ten specific healthy restaurants that don't cost a fortune, including Happy Zoe Vegan Bakery in Greenpoint and Motley Kitchen in the South Bronx.

"The City of Art and Culture" paired an interview with two working PhotoVogue photographers, Chiemeka Offor and Andrew Kung, on how Fresh York City shapes their work and their sense of identity and place.

"A Local's Tale", written by Alice Popovych, profiled Tai Garcia, Community Program Manager at CondéFuture. It followed her into the penthouse of the Brooklyn Museum of Art's director, whose walls happened to be covered in work by the artist Kehinde Wiley, who she unexpectedly got to meet in person! "Turns out that we walked into the home of the man that runs the entire Brooklyn Museum of Art," Garcia said. "There was the most beautiful artwork, paintings, sculptures, all on his walls, and you could get so close to them, closer than you could get in a regular museum.".

Industry observers note that other spreads included "A Day in the Life," a Polaroid-style photo collage of what the students describe as the real New York experience, and "Afterschool Activities," a guide to where city kids actually go to eat or hang out after 9th period (though for this cohort, that's sometimes the Condé Nast office at the World Trade Center). One spread was a parody ad, a riff on the city's old Dunkin' campaign reading "NYC Runs on Dunkin'." Their video was an interview with the owner of one of the city's legendary frozen dessert stands — Delicioso Coco Helado — who told the story of how her father got the idea after seeing similar stands in Puerto Rico, and how they've since become a quintessential piece of New York City childhood, bringing people together across different neighborhoods.

In a recent development, dawn, the senior copy editor who worked with several teams on their drafts, had high praise for this project. "I'm a lifelong New Yorker, and one of the pieces I loved so much was a story about getting to know New York, all the different boroughs, through food and the authenticity of food as culture. Not only did I get a list of restaurants to check out, I felt like the flavor of that story jumped off the page. They were teaching me about a city I've loved for decades." She'd read it as an early draft and saw it through many edits. "It started strong and ended stronger," she stated, pointing to how the team tied in Veselka and the way that community has rallied around the restaurant since Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

Creative Director Olivia DiGennaro, Digital Director Ryan Martinez, Design Director Jasmeryn Reynoso and Features Editor Sydney Liu built this special edition around the theme "Everlasting, Evergreen." Their own mission statement opened the problem: Vanity Fair has covered culture, fashion, and current affairs since 1913, and the team wanted to explore how style today continually draws on and reimagines the eras before it, while pushing back on the idea that only certain kinds of faces belong in a magazine.

Ryan explains the group’s interest in this particular theme: “late 1900s Hollywood celebrity culture has left us with a cycle that is visible and present in today's youth in the form of their interests, inspirations, and most importantly, styles. Our Vanity Fair special edition covers exactly how this evolution takes shape, noticeably in our present society. Just like the brand's heritage, it explores the shift in culture, fashion, and current affairs within our generations (and especially Gen Z) in the past few decades”.

Sources indicate that beyond this, the glitch included a story on how modern pop stars like Sabrina Carpenter and Olivia Dean have drawn on old Hollywood fashion and style ("The Golden Age: Luxurious, Tragic, Longing, the New Sound of Old Hollywood"). The cover story itself interviewed seven NYC teens about how they see their own fashion choices in relation to the eras before them, drawing a line between 20th-century style and how their generation reinterprets it now. The piece was careful to note the difference between influence and imitation: their inspirations, while important, stay that way – just inspirations, not guidelines. The issue closed with a spotlight on Alexandra Dautel, a Paris-based photographer whose work the team mentioned shaped their own photo direction.

Industry observers note that the students’ work over year 1 culminated in an end of year showcase. Their work was presented in a gallery format, with their covers and spreads laid out for guests to browse through. Amongst these guests were alumni from CondéFuture's earlier cohorts who came back to see what the newly introduced group had accomplished.

Students were also able to present their work to the guests, talking them through their journey. Walter Doyle, Senior Education Manager, explained that “the CondéFuture showcase highlights all that the students have absorbed in such a short time. The presentations were incredible, with each capturing the spirit of the brand they were representing”.

As students head into their second year, they are faced with a different kind of project ahead of them: rather than working in teams, each will be paired one-to-one with a mentor for an individual capstone project, applying what this year taught them about how a media career actually works.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a newly introduced pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

Find more Rachel Gurjar recipes here.

Recent findings suggest that to a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It feels like a scene out of a sci-fi movie: Joaquin Phoenix is standing across from me, instructing me to speak into his eyeglasses in a foreign language.

According to recent reports, “Let’s see what happens,” the Oscar winner notes. “It could be any language.”.

According to recent reports, the idea we’re testing here is whether the glasses Phoenix is wearing—a dark-rimmed pair from the South Korean luxury eyewear brand Gentle Monster’s new Intelligent Eyewear collection—could live-translate these words into English. This is one of the glasses’ capabilities the actor was most delighted to discover while he was shooting their campaign film directed by another Oscar winner, Jonathan Glazer. The glasses were crafted in partnership with Google and Samsung, and feature AI-powered technology.

Joaquin Phoenix in the Jonathan Glazer-directed campaign spot.

The last time Phoenix appeared in a fashion campaign, it was 1997 and he was modeling moody suits for Prada. This time around, he stars in the Glazer-directed spot that Phoenix claims was partially inspired by the 1969 documentary Salesman, in which vendors travel across Upcoming England selling Bibles. In the Gentle Monster ad, Phoenix’s character—who has an intense, quasi-manic energy—ventures into an unnamed hotel, where he falls into a deep sleep and meets colorful, large creatures at the end of a hallway. (One might even call them…Gentle Monsters.) Per a press release, the “intelligent eyewear becomes his way of understanding their language and communicating with them, opening up unexpected possibilities for connection.”.

Phoenix had wanted to work with Glazer for a long time. “I’ve known him for years, and when we all approached him, we came up with this really interesting and offbeat idea that just [had so] much mood. He just gets super excited and inspired,” the actor says. During the shoot, the Zone of Interest filmmaker kept the camera rolling for prolonged periods of time, encouraging Phoenix to harness different emotions. A moment in the ad might last for “30 seconds, but we shot for 15 minutes,” he explains. “A whole range of things are happening in those 15 minutes, things that we were trying.”.

Industry observers note that in an email, Glazer reiterated that he was glad to have had a reason to work with Phoenix: “The first image I had was him asleep, maybe dreaming, with the glasses all wonky across his face. The rest kind of grew from there,” the director said.

When I meet the actor last Wednesday at 23 Wall Street in Manhattan—where Gentle Monster has staged an enormous activation for the Intelligent Eyewear launch, complete with fake horses with wagging tails and huge surreal sculptures—it’s hard not to think about his turn in the 2013 film Her, one of the most prophetic AI movies of our time. In the Spike Jonze near-future drama, Phoenix’s character, Theodore Twombly, chats with and subsequently falls for an AI-powered operating system voiced by Scarlett Johansson. If 2011’s Contagion foreshadowed the COVID-19 pandemic, Her’s depiction of chatbots feels eerily similar to the world of ChatGPT dots, Meta Muses, Claude Duets, and Gemini Sparks that we’re beginning to grow accustomed to.

Phoenix and his partner, actress Rooney Mara, wearing Intelligent Eyewear at the Gentle Monster event in Manhattan.

When I ask Phoenix if filming the campaign made him think of Her, he shrugs. “I wasn’t. It seems like I should have,” he says. “It’s funny because I think that sometimes films have more of, maybe, an impact on the people that view them than for me, but I hadn’t thought about that. Somebody just made a joke about it actually, and I was like, ‘Oh yeah, you’re right.’”.

Phoenix, who most recently starred in 2025’s politically tinged neo-Western Eddington, leaves on his Intelligent Eyewear glasses—which are Gemini-embedded, sleek, and thick-rimmed—while we speak.

“The thing is,” he says, “I’m not even aware that I’m wearing them.”.

Recent findings suggest that this recipe is inspired by the garam masala my mother used to make back in India. Just a pinch adds incredible depth and flavor to both meat and vegetable dishes—it’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional. And now you can use it too! This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again. If you prefer a sweeter blend, add more cinnamon and fennel seeds; if you want a spicier kick, increase the black pepper and cloves.

Find more Rachel Gurjar recipes here.

1 hour (plus 1 hour for marinating).

It has been revealed that in a small bowl, toss 12 dried bay leaves, 12 whole cloves, 5 black cardamom pods, 4 whole star anise pods, three 3" (7.5-cm) cinnamon sticks, 1 whole nutmeg, 3 Tbsp. coriander seeds, 3 Tbsp. whole mace fronds, 2 Tbsp. cumin seeds, 1 Tbsp. black peppercorns, and 2 tsp. white poppy seeds to combine.

Sources indicate that heat a medium dry skillet over low heat until hot. Add the spice mixture and toast until slightly fragrant, about 45 seconds. Transfer back to the bowl and let cool.

Transfer the whole nutmeg to a mortar and break into smaller pieces with a pestle (this is just to make it easier to grind, so don’t worry about being too precise!). Repeat with the cinnamon. Tear the bay leaves into smaller pieces. Transfer all of the spices to a spice grinder and grind into a fine powder (it will be slightly warm when you remove the lid). Transfer to an airtight container (do not cover yet) and let cool completely. Then close the lid.

Industry observers note that do Ahead: Garam masala can be made 1 month ahead. Cover and store in a cool, dark place.

To a small heatproof bowl, add 1 medium yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, 2 Tbsp. lime juice, 2 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 2 tsp. chaat masala, ½ tsp. cayenne powder, and ½ tsp. fine sea salt.

In a small pan over medium-high heat, warm 2 Tbsp. peanut oil or any vegetable oil or avocado oil until it shimmers. Add 1 tsp. cumin seeds and cook until fragrant and they start to turn brown, about 1 minute. Be careful not to let the seeds burn or they will taste bitter. Remove from the heat and pour the hot oil over the onions. Toss to coat the onions in the spice mixture.

Serve immediately or let cool and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

It has been revealed that to a mortar and pestle or food processor, add one 2" (5-cm) piece fresh ginger, chopped, 4 garlic cloves, peeled, and 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, chopped, and pound or pulse into a chunky paste. To a medium bowl, add 2 lb. (910 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, excess fat trimmed, cut into 2" [5-cm] pieces, along with the ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp. fine sea salt and toss to combine. Cover and place in the refrigerator to marinate for a minimum of 1 hour or overnight.

In a recent development, in a medium heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-low heat, warm ⅓ cup (80 ml) vegetable oil or avocado oil, then add 1 tsp. cumin seeds, ½ tsp. black mustard seeds, ½ tsp. black peppercorns, 5 whole cloves, 1 fresh or dried bay leaf, 1 star anise, and one 3" [7.5-cm] cinnamon stick, broken into small pieces, and lightly toast and until fragrant, about 1 minute. Increase the heat to medium, add 1 medium red or yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), finely chopped, cover, and cook until the onion is translucent and beginning to turn brown around the edges, stirring halfway through, about 10 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that add 1 Tbsp. ground coriander, 1 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 1 Tbsp. Garam Masala, 2 tsp. cayenne powder, and 1 tsp. powdered turmeric. Stir to combine and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Drain off the excess marinade from the chicken, then add it to the pot along with 3 Tbsp. tomato paste, 1 Tbsp. packed fresh fenugreek leaves, and remaining 1½ tsp. fine sea salt and stir until everything is mixed thoroughly and the chicken is covered with the spices and tomato paste. Add ½ cup (120 ml) water and mix again. Cover and cook until the chicken is cooked through and tender, 30 minutes, stirring halfway through.

In a recent development, remove from the heat and sprinkle with the remaining 1 tsp. Garam Masala, remaining 1 tsp. fresh fenugreek leaves, and cilantro leaves. Serve immediately with lime wedges, Insanely Addictive Pickled Onions, and steamed rice or Indian flatbread.

Do Ahead: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or in the freezer for up to 1 month.

8 Pantry Items Pro Organizers Say You Should Toss ASAP

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (832 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, delish editors handpick every product we feature.
  • No one wants to waste perfectly good food—I’m more likely to eat something slightly past its expiration date than throw it out prematurely—but some pantry items are just taking up space.
  • Dusty canned foods, old spices, expired baking ingredients, and more past-their-prime goods serve little to no culinary value.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

No one wants to waste perfectly good food—I’m more likely to eat something slightly past its expiration date than throw it out prematurely—but some pantry items are just taking up space.

Dusty canned foods, old spices, expired baking ingredients, and more past-their-prime goods serve little to no culinary value. Getting rid of them will actually help you identify the pantry items that you can still use before they go bad. But how can you keep your pantry organized more regularly, and what exactly should you throw away?

It has been revealed that go through every item in your pantry at least twice a year, recommends Nicole Gabai, professional organizer, founder of B. Organized, and author of The Art of Organizing: An Artful Guide to an Organized Life.

If a twice-yearly check-in feels too daunting, consider a weekly five-minute check-in to discard expired goods, says Shaniece Jones, professional organizer and founder of Closet Therapy. “Organize by accessibility and intention,” she says. “Keep your daily go-tos at eye level, heavy items like large cans of oil and bottled water on lower shelves, and seasonal or rarely used items up high.” Labels, Lazy Susans, and drawer dividers are some of her go-to tools for organizing the pantry.

As you start cleaning, check off the following items—these are some of the most common pantry items our organizing experts find past their prime.

It has been revealed that while many shelf-stable foods, such as canned goods, are still safe to eat past their expiration date, you should still check for signs of spoilage. “You can tell canned goods have spoiled if they are rusted, or if you see the cans bulge or dent,” Gabai says.

Sources indicate that labeling pantry items helps you check how long they’ve been open. For opened packages and bulk goods you’ve decanted into containers, write the date on the label so you know when you opened them.

Spices that have lost their smell? Time to go. “If it smells flat or just not aromatic, then it needs to be replaced since it will add very little, if any, flavor to what you’re cooking,” Gabai states. She also notes that ground spices typically last one to two years, while dried herbs can last up to three years.

“Baking ingredients like flour, baking powder, and baking soda can lose their effectiveness over time,” says Meaghan Kessman, founder of Meaghan Kessman Home Organization.

Eventually, flour will go bad, but how long it takes to get rancid depends on how it’s stored and the type of flour. In general, Gabai says it will last at room temperature for six to eight months. She recommends storing it in an airtight container in the fridge or freezer.

It has been revealed that “Check for expiration dates and any signs of spoilage, such as clumping or an off smell,” Kessman states. “If you’re unsure, test baking powder by adding a teaspoon to hot water—if it bubbles, it’s still good to use.”.

We often buy cooking oils in bulk, but keep in mind that they eventually go bad. “Oils and fats, such as olive oil, vegetable oil, and shortening, can become rancid if stored for too long. Rancid oils have a sour or off smell,” Kessman claims. “Always check the expiration date and store oils in a cool, dark place to keep them fresh longer.”.

Gabai recommends storing oils in a cool, dark place and disposing of them properly; freeze in a zip-top bag, then toss in the trash (never pour down the drain).

It has been revealed that these pantry staples are oil-rich, so they spoil faster than you might think. “They can last about 6 months at room temperature, but if you freeze them, they can last a year or more,” Gabai says.

According to recent reports, “Snacks and cereals can go stale promptly once opened,” Kessman notes. She recommends checking expiration dates and signs of staleness, like an unusual smell or texture.

According to Gabai, grains, rice, and beans can last about one to two years, but brown rice and other whole grains will not last as long because of their higher oil content.

Industry observers note that “Condiments like ketchup, mustard, and salad dressings often get pushed to the back of the pantry and forgotten,” Kessman says. “Check for expiration dates and any signs of separation, discoloration, or off smells.”.

In a recent development, honey is the rare exception that probably isn't spoiled. The National Honey Board states that honey has a shelf life of approximately two years, although it can last much longer if stored correctly in a sealed container.

“Honey was found in the tombs of kings and royalty as far back as 3,000 years in Egypt—and it was still edible!” Gabai notes.

If you notice crystallization, Gabai recommends gently heating the honey container in a pot of water.

According to recent reports, each year in Paris, promising young designers present their work to industry legends, hoping to distinguish themselves as part of fashion’s rising fresh guard—and to secure a cash prize of €400,000. Today, applications for the 14th edition of the LVMH Prize are now open.

Over the length of the Prize, the event has served as an invaluable launchpad for independent designers, including two former contestants who are both set to make historic debuts. Grace Wales Bonner (winner, 2016) will present her first collection for Hermès men’s in January, 2027, and just last week, Martine Rose (semifinalist, 2017) was confirmed for the top job at Balenciaga following Pierpaolo Piccioli’s departure. Meanwhile, this year’s Karl Lagerfeld prize winner, Zane Li of Lii, also snagged the top prize at the 2026 CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund.

Jury members, who this year included newbies Michael Rider of Celine and Louis Vuitton CEO Pietro Beccari, are interested in fostering designers with promising businesses. “The jury this time around was very focused on where people produce, where they distribute, and who the final client is,” said Delphine Arnault in an interview following Julie Kegel’s 2026 win. “They were interested in designers who [could talk about] who their [customers] are.”.

Recent findings suggest that designers can submit their application on lvmhprize.com from now through April 4, 2027. Winners of the Karl Lagerfeld Prize and Savoir-Faire Prize, will each take home €200,000, while the three winners of the LVMH Prize for Young Graduates will join the creative studios of the Group’s Houses on one-year contracts. Both the graduate winners and their schools will also receive a €10,000 allocation. Applicants must be between the ages of 18-40 and have created at least two ready-to-wear collections. The semifinals will take place in Paris on March 3 and 4, 2027.

In our Cooking With Friends series, friends of Delish visit the Test Kitchen to share their favorite recipes with you. Happy cooking!

This is my mom’s recipe, and it taught me what simple abundance really looks like. She’d grate tomatoes and spoon the sauce over her native South African pap (a dish made from cornmeal, similar to grits or polenta), rice, ground beef, or almost anything that needed a little love. I couldn’t believe something so good could come from a handful of ingredients, and she showed me that with this dish it’s not about adding more, but how you handle what you have.

It has been revealed that the magic is in the grating. It separates the sweet tomato pulp and leaves the skins behind, giving you the pure heart of the fruit. Please don’t skip the beef bouillon—it gives the sauce its deeper savory backbone. I love this tossed with freshly made spaghetti or tagliatelle, though dried pasta works beautifully, too—exactly like my mom makes it. You can enjoy this year-round, but it’s especially delightful in summer, when tomatoes taste like the sun.

Cranberry Meringue Pie

📅 01 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (980 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A big, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd.
  • Sources indicate that we never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper.
  • Industry observers note that welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A big, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd. The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Use our Perfect Pie Crust as the base to create a sturdy-flaky foundation, and be sure to start the pie the day before you plan to serve it, as the curd requires several hours of chilling to set into a sliceable texture. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

Sources indicate that we never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper. Our favorite is from Gestura. Use the scraper to cut butter, fold dough and nudge it into shape, transfer it from counter to plastic wrap, trim edges, cut strips, and, sure, scrape flour off your counter.

Industry observers note that welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling).

Whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

It has been revealed that make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Recent findings suggest that turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Recent findings suggest that place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too promptly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

According to recent reports, bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

Transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Recent findings suggest that just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

According to recent reports, spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

#19613. This Buzzy Latest Wellness Retreat in Kerala Blends Ancient Traditions With Modern Medicine

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2185 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Vogue ↗ Open Full Page

This Buzzy Latest Wellness Retreat in Kerala Blends Ancient Traditions With Modern Medicine

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2185 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the birthplace of yoga and its sister science Ayurveda, India certainly has no shortage of wellness retreats.
  • Industry observers note that that’s why I was immediately intrigued when I heard about Tulåh Clinical Wellness, a longevity-focused wellness center in Kerala that opened earlier this year and blends ancient Ayurveda with more modern diagnostic testing.
  • It has been revealed that to find out, I booked a weeklong program at Tulåh in early September, right at the tail end of monsoon season (actually considered one of the best times for Ayurvedic treatments in Kerala).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the birthplace of yoga and its sister science Ayurveda, India certainly has no shortage of wellness retreats. The country is quite literally filled with spiritual centers, located everywhere from the foothills of the Himalayas to the beaches of Goa to the sacred riverbanks of Varanasi. I’ve been fortunate enough to visit a fair amount of them over the past decade, thanks to both my work as the author of Destination Wellness, an exploration of ancient health traditions around the world, and the fact that my husband is a born-and-raised Delhiite. We live in Upcoming York, but go to India regularly to stay with family and travel around the rest of the country together.

Industry observers note that that’s why I was immediately intrigued when I heard about Tulåh Clinical Wellness, a longevity-focused wellness center in Kerala that opened earlier this year and blends ancient Ayurveda with more modern diagnostic testing. While some wellness retreats in India are already known for their mix of global healing traditions (Six Senses Vana and Ananda in the Himalayas come to mind), Tulåh’s blend sounded newly introduced to me, closer to a clinical European med spa—albeit one steeped in traditional medicine. Its location stood out to me, too, given Kerala’s long history as the epicenter of Ayurveda in India. I’ve done two very traditional Ayurvedic retreats in Kerala myself, so as I read Tulåh’s extensive list of modern medical offerings—from MRIs to mammograms—I became increasingly curious about its approach. How would all that new testing and technology fit into the longstanding wellness scene in Kerala? And what would that mean for India at large?

It has been revealed that to find out, I booked a weeklong program at Tulåh in early September, right at the tail end of monsoon season (actually considered one of the best times for Ayurvedic treatments in Kerala). It was drizzling when I got off the plane in the coastal city of Calicut, but by the time I arrived at the property half an hour later, the rain had stopped and the air smelled fresh—and not just because of the post-shower skies. Tulåh is set on 30 acres of rewilded forest and medicinal gardens in the Western Ghats, a lush mountain range whose abundance of healing herbs and plants perfumes its air with a consistently earthy scent.

My stay began with a watermelon elixir welcome drink and a tour of the property, which felt even more global than I expected—almost like an international wellness campus with a serious Indian pedigree. That’s partly because “the sanctuary,” as the staffers lovingly call it, is modeled after Auroville, an experimental, spiritually-minded community just north of Pondicherry in Tamil Nadu. Auroville brings people from different countries and cultures together with the goal of living in harmony, and Tulåh—which means “balance” in Sanskrit—has that same world-blending vibe. Designed by Dubai-based firm Lami Architects, the 65-suite property is built on the site of a former cotton mill and looks strikingly modern from the outside, with sleek, flowing curves inspired by the legendary Zaha Hadid. Yet inside its nine main buildings, the minimalist interiors focus largely on Indian craftsmanship, featuring smooth terrazzo floors sourced from artisans in Rajasthan, handwoven earth-toned rugs and marble from Uttar Pradesh, and plush furniture from a design studio in Kerala. Strolling around the grounds after my initial tour, I even heard the upbeat “Qui Es-Tu?” from the French electro-pop duo Poom playing on speakers placed throughout the tropical gardens, followed by a bamboo flutist performing peaceful South Indian Carnatic meditations in the lobby just a few minutes later.

This deliberate mix of influences is the brainchild of founder Faizal Kottikollon, an entrepreneur, engineer, and philanthropist who was born in Kerala, studied in the US, and later settled in Dubai. “Yoga and Ayurveda are India’s IP, but Ayurveda often gets siloed,” he told me one afternoon over a cup of herbal tea. “It gets marketed as an alternative therapy in the medical world, when it should be in the mainstream alongside other modern practices.”.

He, of all people, would know. Back in 2022, Kottikollon was diagnosed with spinal cord compression, and his doctors recommended a very risky spinal surgery. He didn’t want to do that, so he turned instead to the traditional Ayurvedic practices he’d grown up around in Kerala. Ayurvedic practitioner Dr. Vishnuraj Prakash, whom Kottikollon later hired as the first doctor at Tulåh, suggested he do a 21-day panchakarma treatment along with mamsa kizhi massages with warm cloth bundles of goat meat, milk, rice, and various herbs. In Ayurveda, goat meat is thought to strengthen muscle tissues—and by all accounts it did. Kottikollon’s next MRI showed that his compression was healed. Today, he says he is 99% recovered.

“When we did the MRI after my panchakarma, my modern medicine doctors had to believe in Ayurveda, because the proof was right there,” he told me. “And that’s when I said, ‘Oh my god, this is the future of healthcare.’ Ayurveda had the solution to my problem for thousands of years, but my modern doctors never knew. That’s why it should be integrated with modern medicine rather than working on its own. People don’t talk to each other, because human beings are blocked by egos—but all doctors need to work together. And that’s what I’m trying to change.”.

The multidisciplinary team at Tulåh.

Sources indicate that his proposal (and his $100 million investment) seems to be working. At Tulåh, my days were filled with a true mix of traditional Ayurvedic practices and modern longevity diagnostics. It all started, as these sorts of retreats so often do, well before my stay, when I sent in various samples for the medical team to assess just a few months after their February opening. Then I went straight into two full days of diagnostic tests and consultations the day after I arrived. A nurse took my blood sample on my first morning, followed by a BCA (body composition analysis) and an Ayurvedic consultation with my designated practitioner, Dr. Urvashi Naithani. She read my pulse, asked some lifestyle questions, and ultimately identified a kapha imbalance in my system that was making me sluggish. In Ayurveda, everyone has a unique constitution shaped by three doshas: vata (air and space), pitta (fire and water), and kapha (earth and water). The goal in life is to keep all three doshas in balance at all times, though as I can attest, that’s very hard to do.

A shirodhara treatment on a Vichy Shower Bed.

My program continued with a couple of kapha-reducing Ayurvedic treatments interspersed with more modern longevity testing. That included a chest X-ray, a CAC scan, a DXA scan, an MRI (quite an accomplishment for a claustrophobe like me), a dental appointment, a psychological assessment, and a slew of mobility and fitness consultations. At times it felt a bit jarring to go from a soothing ancient therapy like shirodhara to a terrifying 45-minute scan in a metal tube, but I always knew it was all in pursuit of self-knowledge—and that made me feel really good. It was almost like being back in school, only the subject was myself.

According to recent reports, everything eventually culminated with the major “MDM meeting,” or the multidisciplinary team meeting, on my third full day. This meeting is essentially Kottikollon’s vision of integration come to life: when representatives from Tulåh’s nine departments (Ayurveda, functional medicine, modern medicine, Chinese medicine, fitness, physiotherapy, psychology, clinical yoga, and dental) convene to discuss your results and put together a custom initiative for the rest of your stay and your routine after you leave. Back to the school metaphor, I couldn’t help but think of it as all my teachers from different subjects gossiping about me in the conference room… but with only my very best interests in mind.

According to recent reports, if the team had determined I needed serious medical attention, Tulåh has an on-site ICU and operating room, as well as access to a nearby hospital that Kottikollon also owns. But in my case, the consensus across the board was that I simply needed to boost my energy and get much, much stronger. One of the biggest subjects the MDM team discusses is your Tulåh Life Index, a proprietary number they calculate to assess your body’s overall function based on your bloodwork, body composition results, lifestyle questions, and more. My score was 71 out of 100, which was not terrible (70 and above is the goal), but not great either—thanks largely to my lack of muscle mass. In my defense, there was a good reason for that. As I told the doctors during my consultations, I stopped strength training regularly during a five-year period of IVF treatments, when fertility doctors advise against lifting weights because of the risk of ovarian torsion. Though I could’ve done more strength training between IVF rounds, I was still a bit too scared for my ovaries to fully get back into it. Now that I’m finally emerging from the IVF tunnel thanks to turning to surrogacy, the doctors recommended I make regaining my muscle mass a top priority—especially since I’m now 41, when these things begin to matter even more. I knew this already, technically, but hearing it from a team of professionals based on my own numbers made it feel extra real to me—and all the more urgent.

According to recent reports, what followed was a few more packed days of treatments and meals customized to my new high-strength, high-energy lifestyle. My meals were delicious—lots of high-protein South Indian fish curries and North Indian specialties like chicken tikka and chana masala, all made with predominantly organic and locally-grown ingredients. And unlike my past Ayurvedic retreats in Kerala, where the strategy mostly revolved around oil treatments and yoga, therapies at Tulåh also included aquatic fitness, personal strength training sessions, clinical yoga with a focus on alignment, and daily sound baths in the incredible Sonorium (I fell asleep every time). Throughout it all, the staff was so caring and lovely as well. During a qawwali performance in the Sonorium one night, I even saw a young teacher offer an older Indian uncle a pillow for behind his back without him ever asking.

My Ayurvedic treatments were still my favorite, though. In a plot twist that will undoubtedly delight all Ayurveda lovers, Kottikollon and his team have combined the Vichy shower—named after the thermal spa town of Vichy, France—with a traditional Ayurvedic massage bed to create the recently patented Vichy Shower Bed, which has six showerheads directly above the heated, ergonomically designed table. This means that, rather than shuffling you to the shower after your treatment so you can rinse off all the medicated oil, practitioners do it for you right there on the bed—including a shampoo and condition. In my experience, Ayurvedic oil is often near impossible to get off, so this perk was absolute bliss for me. And it’s one that Kottikollon hopes will make Ayurveda more accessible to the mainstream as well. “Traditional wooden Ayurvedic beds can be slippery and leave you with oil all over, and I believe this is part of the reason why Ayurveda has not been adopted in the current world,” he told me. “But Ayurveda can solve so many problems—which is why I want this bed to be at all the spas and hospitals in the world along with all the other options.”.

A treatment room with a Vichy Shower Bed.

I’ll co-sign that. While I wasn’t sure how it would feel to combine Ayurveda with all things modern, I ended up loving the 360-degree approach. Not having to pick a lane (or a century) was so convenient—like one-stop shopping for longevity. If anything, seeing the ancient practices I’ve come to love used as part of a diagnostics-informed treatment strategy even helped me appreciate them in a latest, deeper way.

I’m also happy to report I’ve followed through on my strength and energy mission, at least somewhat, since I checked out of Tulåh a month ago. As a frequent traveler, it’s hard for me to get into a super steady routine, but I did lift weights at my hotel gym in Japan last week as opposed to just running on the treadmill—and that felt like progress to me. At home in New York, I’ve also been consulting Tulåh’s Home app, which provides personalized recipes, workout plans, yoga poses and meditations based on my medical results. I don’t use it every day (maybe you’ve heard of a little thing called the NYC restaurant scene?), but I’ve made enough of the recipes to tell you they’re easy and good. And the yoga nidra meditation has become my new go-to for getting out of an afternoon slump.

It has been revealed that we have a saying in my family of journalists: “Everything’s been noted, but not everyone has said it.” And so, in the grand tradition of honoring your roots, allow me to state the obvious: Knowledge really is power. It feels so good to know exactly what I need to do. Now I just need to keep doing it.

Industry News: David Corenswet Wore a Cult-Favorite Seiko on the Red Carpet

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Superman actor David Corenswet, who’s set to reprise his Man of Steel role in Man of Tomorrow next year, just wore a way-out-of-left-field watch with a tuxedo during the 17th Governors Awards last night.
  • Industry observers note that the “Pogue,” as the yellow-dial variant is known, is a wildly cool and beloved watch, and Corenswet smartly took advantage of the way it pops against the black-and-white of a classic tux.
  • What’s so special about the 6139, and why is it called the “Pogue,” you might ask?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Superman actor David Corenswet, who’s set to reprise his Man of Steel role in Man of Tomorrow next year, just wore a way-out-of-left-field watch with a tuxedo during the 17th Governors Awards last night. There was no mistaking the glint of its dial from across the step-and-repeat: a Seiko ref. 6139 "Pogue" automatic chronograph. The bulky sport watch looked totally out of place in the restrained, elegant atmosphere of the awards ceremony…and absolutely perfect.

Industry observers note that the “Pogue,” as the yellow-dial variant is known, is a wildly cool and beloved watch, and Corenswet smartly took advantage of the way it pops against the black-and-white of a classic tux. Plus, it doesn’t hurt that among Seiko collectors, the Pogue is a cult classic, often ranking towards the top of best-Seiko-ever lists. Not only is it an aesthetic swerve on the red carpet, but it’s the type of relatively affordable oddball celebrities rarely reach for.

What’s so special about the 6139, and why is it called the “Pogue,” you might ask? The 6139 was among the very first batch of automatic chronographs. A group of brands—Seiko; a consortium of Hamilton-Büren, Heuer-Leonaids, Breitling, and Dubois Dépraz; and Zenith-Movado—raced to be the first to debut the mechanical innovation. Who won the race is still a matter of debate, but one thing is for certain: when the 6139 hit the Japanese market in 1969, it featured an integrated design, a column wheel, and a vertical clutch. Meshing hallmarks of classic chronograph construction with the convenience of automatic winding at a relatively affordable price, it was paired with a wide variety of colorful dials and funky cases and produced for roughly a decade.

A 1972 advertisement for the Pogue.

Recent findings suggest that one of these designs, the ref. 6139-6002, is particularly eye-catching thanks to its bright-yellow dial with a contrasting blue-and-red tachymeter bezel, a 30-minute chronograph register, and a day-date display. American astronaut Col. William R. famously wore the Pogue during the Skylab 4 mission from November 1973 to February 1974. Subsequently, the 6139-6002 took on Pogue’s name, and is now one of the most collectible vintage Seiko references.

The best part? Though there’s unfortunately no magic bullet to make you 6’4” and handsome as Superman, you can snag a pretty good “Pogue” for under $2,000. It may not take you into space, but as Corenswet has proven, it sure livens up your average black-tie outfit.

A Chef’s Guide to Eating and Drinking in Santo Domingo

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, on a Friday night in July, Nidia Evangelista walked with her arms crossed over the Puente Flotante toward East Santo Domingo.
  • On the other side, we turned a corner and found hundreds gathered around a dance floor in the undercroft of a bigger bridge.
  • It has been revealed that bur normally walks (or bikes) everywhere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, on a Friday night in July, Nidia Evangelista walked with her arms crossed over the Puente Flotante toward East Santo Domingo. Six lanes of traffic jockeyed inches from her left shoulder, while the black waters of the Río Ozama coursed below. “Oh my God, Oli, what are we doing?” she stated. “Nobody does this.” Evangelista is the communications manager for Santo Domingo’s most intriguing restaurant, Casarré. Her boss, Swiss Dominican chef Olivier Bur, was leading Evangelista, photographer Clay Williams, and me beyond the fortified walls of the Zona Colonial, where few travel on foot.

On the other side, we turned a corner and found hundreds gathered around a dance floor in the undercroft of a bigger bridge. Live bachata drowned out the traffic overhead. Bur procured a big bottle of Presidente and plastic cups from a vendor, poured, and raised a “Salud!”.

It has been revealed that bur normally walks (or bikes) everywhere. Moving slowly, he’s learned the textures of the city. Still, for the next six days, he took Williams and me to his most beloved restaurants by car. We visited a string of chimi stands where hawkers compete for clientele through the night; a chicharrón spot where couples dance shoeless on the cool tile floor; and a cafeteria where boys shuffle stewed eggplant, beets, and goat to bus drivers en route. Places like these are the “infrastructure for life,” Bur said. “Thirty years ago, there was nothing else.”.

According to recent reports, over the last couple of decades, however, another dining scene has sprouted. Dominican chefs have returned from kitchens in Mexico, Japan, or Switzerland to explore the forgotten and sometimes shunned ingredients of their (or their parents’) homes. They served us conch, cassava, breadfruit, and djon-djon mushrooms in sashimis, foams, tostones, and surprising dessert creams. The dishes were fresh and exciting, but local and global traditions have always mingled—as such, the cuisine is not “New Dominican,” it’s simply “Dominican,” fully expressed.

Calle Andrés Julio Aybar 13+1 829 545 7503.

The Piantini neighborhood was once verdant and sleepy, according to Bur. Now it’s a bustling business district. Most of the remaining vegetation decorates the façades of restaurants, like Ajualä’s. Brushed palm thatch and a bushy barba de Fidel (Fidel’s beard) tree greet you at the tall aged-steel door.

It has been revealed that venezuelan chef Saverio Stassi is a leader among the culinary fresh guard. His treatment of local ingredients is virtuosic. He confits guinea hen in cocoa butter and tops breadfruit tostones with local yellowfin and Cambita avocado; and over two days, his team bathes the succulent goat from the northwest—where they famously graze on wild oregano, self-infusing their meat—in Seville orange juice before roasting it in a barbacoa pit.

Calle Max Henríquez Ureña 14+1 809 547 3592.

Sources indicate that chef Erik Malmsten has cooked at his parents’ cabaret in Gothenburg, Sweden, at Aquavit in Newly introduced York, and at Bocuse d’Or competitions around the world. But to take his career to the next level, he returned to his mother’s homeland to open a Nordic-Japanese restaurant.

“You’ll see, it’s really good,” Bur told us. The meal starts with “lobster chicharrón,” with a reduced crustacean bisque, fried into airy orange sheets of bubbly crackling and served with tōgarashi Kewpie. Then, a parade of sashimi, like king fish, served with brown butter soy emulsion, ikura, and lemon zest. It ends with Dominican chocolates, molded, painted, and plated to look like koi fish on a synchronized swim.

Calle Caonabo 35+1 809 584 9481.

If, like me, you come from a pizza region, you might not be inclined to use one of your Santo Domingo meal slots on a pie. But I urge you: Make time for Casa Gazcue. Spanish Dominican chef Francis Pena’s 48-hour-fermented crust comes blistered and sometimes covered in honeyed sesame seeds. Iterations are variously laden with spicy Dominican oxtail, chimi sandwich sauce, pistachio, and jamón ibérico, but you don’t have to choose: For groups, he serves a rosca (a round with an open middle) of six sections arranged like floral pizza petals.

Calle Pablo Casals+1 809 562 6060.

Recent findings suggest that in 1954, the Bonarelli family opened the legendary Italian restaurant Vesuvio. For decades, it was the place—the only place—to go out for a formal sit-down meal around here. Vesuvio closed over 20 years ago, but the founder’s grandson, Giancarlo Bonarelli, now runs Bottega Fratelli in a sleek modern building in Naco (Piantini’s equally upscale neighbor).

It has been revealed that you’ll notice a great variety of beet dishes in the Dominican Republic. Farmers harvest them year-round in the cool, pine-forested Costanza Valley. Try them here, roasted and served with blue cheese, chèvre, candied nuts, and honey. Also try a carpaccio of king mackerel, caught off the eastern coast, or any of the risottos, an emblem of the family’s enduring Italian culinary influence.

Calle del Seminario #57+1 809 565 1621.

In a recent development, hideyoshi Tateyama’s parents opened Samurai in 1990. The restaurant joined Vesuvio, along with one or two others in that era’s small restaurant scene. It still stands out today among the many dozens.

Be sure to order the guatapaná con coco. A tried-and-true combo of shrimp and coconut imbued with native guatapaná leaf, tobiko, sesame seed, and scallion—it’s been on the menu for two decades. Also, don’t miss the chance to sample a sashimi of the meter-long “calamar diamante” from the Samaná region. It’s simply brightened with lemon zest. Meals are capped with a green tea amaro. Once a month, Tateyama personally runs a chef’s-choice omakase service.

Avenida Independencia 312+1 809 682 1433.

On the day we visited Villar Hermanos, lines formed around the block for each of two buffets. Women balanced towers of takeout containers tightly wrapped in plastic. It was the World Cup Final, and people were rushing to get some of the city’s best comfort food to their coffee tables. “This is the place to come for all the Dominican classics,” Bur told us.

We found a large table under the sprawling canopy of a banyan tree and ordered mofongo. It was moist, punctuated with crisp chicharrón crackling. The sancocho, the classic Domincan stew thick with potato and yuca starch, assumed extra body when alternating spoonfuls of broth and rice. While I didn’t have my coveted mangú and tres golpes (salami, queso frito, and eggs), I would trade my house and car to live next door and eat breakfast there every morning under the filtered sun.

Avenida San Vicente de Paúl, Santo Domingo Este 11504+1 809 244 8906.

On Avenida San Vicente de Paúl in East Santo Domingo, scooters zip down the busy street all through the night, many popping over a curb into the Plaza Del Chimi. The “plaza” is a stretch of  10 to 15 “chimi” sandwich stalls outfitted with griddles and prep stations heaped with roasted pork shoulders. Dealers promptly slice the meat, lay it on the griddle, flip it onto a squishy pan de agua roll, and top it with cabbage, tomato, and tangy pink sauce before sliding it into your mitts. The stalls are open till 6 a.m. When they run out of beer, a man runs bottles from a cooler at his house and serves them in paper bags.

Avenida Independencia KM 8+1 809 532 2580.

Sources indicate that across from a shopping mall on Avenida Indepencia, about a dozen cars cram into five parking spaces for the lunch or late-night staple pica pollo. Behind a crowded serving station, a woman slides eight pounds of chicken into a hotel pan, and the picking begins. Six sets of tongs compete for room, like bird beaks, snapping the chicken into styrofoam containers before barely holding them shut with strained rubber bands. Another eight pounds comes out less than two minutes later.

Industry observers note that pica pollo is one of the lasting influences of Chinese immigrants in Santo Domingo. Usually cooks marinate it in bitter orange, garlic, and oregano before coating it in flour and spice (in this case we detected Chinese five-spice) and deep-frying it to golden brown.

Avenida Cayetano Germosén+1 809 286 2141.

In a recent development, at Parque Mirador Sur, teens and whole families perch along concrete walls and hilltops eating fried yuca and succulent mojo-dipped chicharrón with long toothpicks. It comes from the crowded, steel-barred serving window across the street: Chicharrones Light de la Cayetano.

Among all the chicharrón we ate in the city (there was a lot), theirs stood out. There’s a small covered seating area where you can order beer to share. Bachata plays loud over a hanging speaker. Women take turns kicking off their heels to do the four-step shimmy with their jevos (boyfriends).

Calle Ciriaco Ramirez 70+1 809 689 5544.

Industry observers note that the Colmado, Bur says, “is essential to Dominican life. Everything happens there.” For 70 years, Colmado La Venganza has anchored a prominent corner in the Don Bosco neighborhood. It’s hosted thousands of late-night domino games and sports viewing parties. We were there during the World Cup.

It has been revealed that at the entrance, a man with a crisp-edged haircut, significant sunglasses, and a pressed floral shirt parked his shoe on a milk crate while a boy polished it with a rag. Inside, groups spanning all ages gathered at high-tops and around the bar. Folks shared triple-stacked ham, pickle, and cheese sandwiches, pressed, cubed, and spiked with toothpicks: the “sándwich especial.” Leaving the bar, chef Raniel Cruz (part of our party) texted his mom in Montreal. She responded: “Wait, you’re at Venganza? I used to drink there.”.

Calle Luperón 52+1 849 460 5600.

Recent findings suggest that one couldn’t understand the Dominican Republic’s vast culinary splendor in a lifetime, but if you had just one night to try, you’d want to dine at Casarré. Every Tuesday, the team takes excursions. We accompanied them to meet the countryside cooks, who wrap guáyiga root masa in leaves from the almond trees on Najayo beach and bake it in coal-covered pots. We visited a produce market, where vendors passed fruit samples, like little red “frutas milagrosas” that, when chewed beforehand, make bitter limes taste like sweet limeade.

At night, in a candlelit, contemplative room in the Zona Colonial, Bur and his team showcase their findings in a series of sublime, thoughtful dishes. On our visit, they presented djon-djon mushrooms from the Haitian borderlands in a sweet, guáyiga-thickened foam and in the broth of a citrusy okra and fish soup. Chef Isabella Sánchez explained: “The broth is murky, like the current state of the Río Ozama. It represents the negative aspects of our water—contamination and conflict—and the beautiful: the fish, the beaches, and our grandmother’s tea.”.

Avenida Lope de Vega 44+1 809 816 7200.

According to recent reports, smoke from an open Uruguayan-style parrilla floats in the soft light over two stories. Our waiter said, “We want this to feel like a Sunday asado.” Indeed, the smoke, the char, and the Malbec are there. This asado, though, also has Negronis smoked tableside and poured from a glass goose. As we awaited a perfect aged rib eye, we enjoyed paper-thin beef carpaccio with foie, and a paella-esque rice with soft leeks, cilantro, and pork trotters.

Recommendations on where to dine, shop, and stay, wherever you’re headed next.

💡 Key Takeaways
