The 5 Healthiest Fast Food Salads, According To Nutritionists

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1084 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, fast food chains aren’t exactly famous for their salads.
  • To identify the best better-for-you fast-food salads, we asked three nutrition experts to weigh in.
  • First, we need to debunk salad’s diet-friendly reputation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, fast food chains aren’t exactly famous for their salads. They usually fall into two categories: a sad bowl of lettuce added to menus as an afterthought, or a vehicle for fried, calorie-dense ingredients that offset any nutritional upsides. But some chains do make an effort to sell salads worth ordering.

To identify the best better-for-you fast-food salads, we asked three nutrition experts to weigh in. Here are the menu items they recommend, along with some tips and tricks for maximizing their nutrition.

First, we need to debunk salad’s diet-friendly reputation. “A salad isn't automatically the healthiest choice on a fast food menu,” says Kathy Levin, RDN, CDCES, dipACLM, LDN. “Once you add fried chicken, bacon, cheese, candied nuts, crunchy toppings, and a creamy dressing, some salads land in the same calorie and fat range as a burger and fries.”.

Taking all of those components away isn’t always a solution either. A sad salad with just lettuce and a smattering of vegetables is more like rabbit food than a satisfying meal for humans. According to Briana V. Reamer, MS, RDN, LDN, the secret is getting enough fiber, which she indicates “will keep you satisfied and full until your next meal.” Take advantage of the restaurant's add-ons—like beans, avocado, and more vegetables—to make your salad more substantial.

Experts also recommend watching your saturated fat intake, specifically with your protein and dressing. Grilled chicken generally has fewer calories and less saturated fat than deep-fried alternatives. Consider your dressing options, too. “If you’re not sure what to pick, look for a vinaigrette or olive-oil-based dressing,” says Tina Sergi, MS, RD, CSSD, CSCS, TSAC-F.

According to recent reports, and, as a rule of thumb, order your dressing on the side. It keeps your salad from getting soggy on the drive home, for one, but it also gives you more portion control. “Using only part of the packet cuts saturated fat and sodium, especially when they're already on the higher end,” Sergi adds.

In a recent development, of course, the dressing is only part of the equation. With those tips in mind, here are the five salads that made the cut.

This regional chain is known for its fire-grilled chicken, and this salad packs plenty of it. Each portion contains a double serving of citrus-marinated chicken breast, sliced avocado, cotija cheese, salsa fresca, and tortilla strips over a bed of greens. It's served with a creamy Mexican-inspired Caesar dressing.

El Pollo Loco strikes the right balance between substantial and light with this dish. Before you add dressing, the entire salad contains 420 calories and 52 grams of protein. “The fire-grilled chicken makes it very filling, the avocado adds heart-healthy fat and fiber, and the salsa fresca adds flavor without much sodium or sugar,” Levin says.

Like with most salads, the dressing significantly raises the calorie count—in this case, it adds 440 calories if you use the entire serving. If you're closely monitoring your daily intake, Levin advises going easy on the dressing.

Industry observers note that culver’s may be best known for its ButterBurgers, but experts say you shouldn’t sleep on its salads. The Chicken Cashew Salad in particular is a great choice. It starts with a bed of mixed greens, topped with cheddar, grape tomatoes, cucumbers, and roasted cashews. You can also choose from several dressings to finish it off.

Sources indicate that with grilled chicken, the salad comes in at 430 calories and 41 grams of protein before adding dressing. Culver’s also offers six dressing varieties ranging from 50 to 260 calories.

It has been revealed that “This is a great fiber- and protein-packed option,” states Sergi. “Plus, the cashews add healthy fats, copper to support energy production, and magnesium for optimal nerve and muscle function.”.

This Lone Star staple sells a Cobb salad that’s a lighter alternative to its lineup of burgers and sandwiches. It comes loaded with all of the essentials: greens, bacon, a hard-boiled egg, grape tomatoes, carrots, and shredded cheese. You can also choose from three chicken options (the grilled chicken filet is, naturally, lighter than the fried options).

Without dressing, Whataburger's Cobb with grilled chicken has 430 calories and 44 grams of protein. It's also a source of fiber and is low in sugar, according to Reamer. “Salads high in fiber help with weight management and satisfy hunger.”.

Some of Whataburger's creamier dressings add 200 to 280 calories, while the balsamic vinaigrette has 180.

Recent findings suggest that for a fried chicken chain, Chick-fil-A makes some surprisingly stellar salads. The Market Salad starts with mixed greens and is topped with strawberries, blueberries, red and green apples, blue cheese, roasted almonds, and the chain’s Harvest Nut Granola. Chick-fil-A also has the most protein options on this list. The grilled chicken can come in nugget or filet form, warm or cold, and spicy or regular. Talk about variety!

According to recent reports, the different grilled chicken options provide between 26 and 32 grams of protein, according to Chick-fil-A's nutrition guide. Levin also says you can forgo chicken entirely for a meatless meal that doesn't feel like an afterthought. “Berries and apples bring fiber, antioxidants and natural sweetness, which makes it one of the most plant-forward options on the list.”.

Sources indicate that the Market Salad is typically paired with Chick-fil-A's Zesty Apple Cider Vinaigrette Dressing, which contains 230 calories per packet. But the chain is known for its sauces, after all, so you can swap it out for another option. There's a Light Balsamic Vinaigrette with 80 calories, Fat-Free Honey Mustard with 90, and Light Italian Dressing with just 25.

Zaxby's is the third chicken chain on this list, and it stands out by offering a salad with Asian-inspired flavors. The Asian Zensation Zalad (not Salad) adds shredded carrots, cabbage, wonton strips, and Asian Slaw to mixed greens, along with a drizzle of teriyaki sauce. It also comes with a vegetable egg roll on the side.

This salad is loaded with plant-based toppings, which is why Levin also recommends the garden version as a vegetarian option. Zaxby's lists that version at 390 calories, while the grilled chicken version comes in at 530 calories and 39 grams of protein, before adding dressing.

According to recent reports, alongside the teriyaki drizzle, Zaxby's offers Citrus Vinaigrette with the salad, which has 110 calories per packet. It's one of the chain's lighter options. But if you're watching your calorie intake, you can swap in Lite Vinaigrette, which contains just 30 calories.

Gravy-Braised Turkey

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (575 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that cooking a whole turkey is a commitment.
  • According to recent reports, this recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now.
  • For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

According to recent reports, this recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.).

It has been revealed that add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Sources indicate that add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Recent findings suggest that nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Sources indicate that let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.).

Recipe by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Here’s how to make Legoland’s legendary apple fries, complete with the cinnamon sugar coating, caramel drizzle and vanilla whipped cream dip.

Legoland’s most popular food isn’t the usual lacy funnel cake or plate of chicken tenders. Look around for the longest line, and you’ll find it at Granny’s Apple Fries, where deep-fried apple sticks are coated in cinnamon-sugar, drizzled with caramel sauce and served with vanilla whipped cream. Thankfully you don’t need to wait in line (or buy a ticket to the park) to enjoy these legendary apple fries. Here’s how to make a copycat version of Legoland’s apple fries right at home, down to the homemade whipped cream and caramel sauce drizzle.

Industry observers note that peel and core the apples. Using a sharp knife, carefully cut the apples into 1/2-inch sticks.

Allison Cebulla For Taste Of Home.

In a recent development, place the cornstarch in a large bowl. Add the apple sticks, a few at a time, tossing to thoroughly coat them. Shake off the excess.

Allison Cebulla For Taste Of Home.

In an electric skillet or deep-fat fryer, heat the oil to 375°. Fry the apple fries, a few at a time, until they’re golden brown. Drain the oil from the apple fries by placing them on paper towels.

In a small bowl, stir together the granulated sugar and cinnamon. Immediately sprinkle the mixture over the hot fries. The sooner you sprinkle, the better the mixture sticks.

Editor’s Tip: Never, ever overcrowd your skillet or deep-fat fryer. Doing so may cause a dangerous boil-over. Always work in small batches.

Allison Cebulla For Taste Of Home.

In a recent development, in a small, chilled glass bowl, use chilled beaters to beat the heavy whipping cream until it begins to thicken. Add the confectioners’ sugar and vanilla extract, and beat until soft peaks form.

Serve the apple fries warm with the vanilla whipped cream. If desired, drizzle the apple fries with warmed caramel sauce.

Allison Cebulla For Taste Of Home.

Allow leftover apple fries to cool completely to room temperature, then store them in an airtight container. They can last in the fridge for up to four days.

Yes, you can freeze apple fries. Allow them to cool to room temperature, then transfer them to an airtight container with pieces of parchment or waxed paper between them. Freeze them for up to two months. Reheat them in a 400° oven until they’re crispy and warmed through.

Allison Cebulla For Taste Of Home.

Recent findings suggest that to cut apples for apple fries, peel and core the apples, then cut them into fourths. From there, cut the apple into 1/2-inch slices lengthwise, then turn each slice on its side and cut it in half lengthwise. You should be left with apple matchsticks.

Industry observers note that if your apple fries are soggy, the oil temperature was likely too low. When the oil isn’t hot enough, it will soak into the cornstarch and make it soggy rather than crisping the fries. It’s a common deep-frying mistake, so make sure to keep a close watch on the oil’s temperature.

Serve apple fries immediately while they’re still hot. We love to finish them with salted caramel sauce and dip them in the vanilla whipped cream. Serve your apple fries with hot apple cider or homemade hot chocolate to make your treat extra decadent and sweet.

Grace Cacciato Wins the 2026–2027 S.Pellegrino Young Chef Academy US Regional Final

💡 Key Takeaways
  • After competing against nine culinary talents from across the country, chef Grace Cacciato was named the winner of the 2026–2027 S.Pellegrino Young Chef Academy US Regional Final.
  • The 10 chefs vying to win the region cooked in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen in Fresh York City on Monday, and the winner was unveiled the following evening at the US Regional Final Gala & Awards.
  • Industry observers note that representing the Michelin-starred restaurant Saga in New York, Cacciato presented a dish that featured the most components of any in the competition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After competing against nine culinary talents from across the country, chef Grace Cacciato was named the winner of the 2026–2027 S.Pellegrino Young Chef Academy US Regional Final. A panel of judges selected her roasted squab with chanterelle mushrooms and toasted buckwheat, black raspberry, and Swiss chard purées to represent the United States at the Grand Finale in Milan.

The 10 chefs vying to win the region cooked in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen in Fresh York City on Monday, and the winner was unveiled the following evening at the US Regional Final Gala & Awards. Everyone enjoyed the Gala menu, crafted by chef Garrett Brower, the 2024–25 US winner who is the chef de cuisine at Bresca in Washington, DC, and global mentor chef Aisha Ibrahim.

Industry observers note that representing the Michelin-starred restaurant Saga in New York, Cacciato presented a dish that featured the most components of any in the competition. All the judges were impressed with her sauce work and bold flavors.

In a recent development, saga executive chef Charlie Mitchell returned for his second year as a mentor, working alongside Cacciato, a repeat competitor. “It was nice to see how her brain works…getting her perspective was inspiring,” he remarked. Cacciato was equally enthusiastic. “It’s the best competition, and everyone wants to be a part of it,” she said.

The chefs had five hours to prepare and execute their signature dishes in the Test Kitchen. With an hour remaining, guests had the opportunity to mingle over food and drinks. Chef Rachel Bindel, a 2022 US Finalist, served rye toast piled high with Maryland blue crab, horseradish crème, and pickled green tomato. Chef Akshay Kumar, a 2024 finalist, tucked Kumamoto oysters into a pani puri with cucumber gel and lemon foam. Tomato pie from Philadelphia’s Pizza Freak Co., spoonfuls of Petrossian caviar, and a selection of wines, S.Pellegrino beverages, and cocktails rounded out the reception.

Nilou Motamed, a culinary expert and Iron Chef judge on Netflix, hosted the competition. Accomplished chefs from several states served as judges: chef and co-owner E.J. Lagasse of Emeril’s in Upcoming Orleans; executive chef and partner Fariyal Abdullahi of Hav & Mar in New York City; Isabel Coss, executive chef at Pascual and founding pastry chef at Lutèce in Washington, DC; Jon Yao, head chef and owner at Kato in Los Angeles; and Ryan Ratino, executive chef and owner at Bresca and Jônt in Washington, DC.

Recent findings suggest that motamed explained that each competitor had spent several months developing their dish alongside a chef mentor. The mentors were in the Test Kitchen throughout the competition, but were not permitted to participate in the cooking. She also outlined the three pillars of the S.Pellegrino Young Chef Academy: Community, Competition, and Mentorship, which support its mission to discover and nurture the next generation of culinary talent.

Recent findings suggest that each chef’s arrival was unveiled by a burst of music and a live video feed from the Test Kitchen, where a fleet of servers collected the finished plates before delivering them to the judges. First up was chef Adolfo Pucci of Michelin-starred Ariete in Miami. His dish, “Three Shores, One Table,” told the story of his Venezuelan heritage, his family’s roots in Southern Italy, and his current home in Miami. The ambitious plate featured a lamb ragù inspired by his grandmother’s cooking and lacto-fermented Florida blueberries.

Chef Amit Kumar of three-Michelin-starred Eleven Madison Park in New York City presented the competition’s only fully vegan dish: “Sunchoke with Banana Blossoms, Chanterelles, and Sherry.” Drawing on memories of the banana trees he grew up with in India, Kumar combined banana blossoms, sunchoke purée, chanterelle mushrooms, and a ragù of sherry and banana flowers to create a hearty and deeply satisfying dish. Judge Fariyal Abdullahi called it “a very successful dish, not just a very successful vegan dish.”.

Representing Auro at Four Seasons Resort and Residences Napa Valley, chef Evan Neumann presented “From the Valley to the Shoreline,” a love letter to the terroir of Northern California and Provence, where he grew up. Kombu-poached wild razor clams mingled with Napa verjuice and coastal seaweeds in a dish the judges found exceptionally creative. Neumann took home the S.Pellegrino Social Responsibility Award for his thoughtful approach to social responsibility and sustainable practices.

At just 21, chef Lucy Field of New York City’s fine dining bastion Per Se was the youngest competitor. Her dish, “Pekin Duck, Cherry, Plum,” was a study in restraint with only six components.

Industry observers note that chef Marcus Osorio, chef de cuisine at Living Room in Los Angeles, drew inspiration from his Salvadoran and Indigenous roots for his “Tamal de Pollo.” The dish featured corn sourced from Somos Maíz, the manufacturer founded by his mentor, chef Ron Oliver, and a mole poblano the two developed together. Judge Isabel Coss noted the challenge of preparing a mole with such limited time, but the judges were impressed by Osorio’s ability to marry European cooking techniques with soulful Indigenous ingredients and flavors.

Chef Nickolas Abbott hails from the small Appalachian town of Waynesville, North Carolina, and leads Chop Shop Butchery in Asheville. At the competition, he told the story of his community on a plate. His “Smoked Pork Loin, Fennel & Cheese Slaw, Sweet Potato, Asparagus, Fried Sausage, Pork Sauce Robert” reflected the people who shaped him, particularly his grandmother, his greatest inspiration as a chef.

Los Angeles–based chef Natasha Daniels of Providence showcased her vegetable-forward, zero-waste approach with “The Whole Bird, The Whole Garden.” The dish incorporated every part of a chicken across four preparations, alongside an array of vegetables and herbs inspired by her time working at The Chef’s Garden.

Daniels received two honors: the Acqua Panna Connection in Gastronomy Award and the Fine Dining Lovers Award. Voted on by regional mentors, the Acqua Panna award recognized the dish that best demonstrated a connection between culinary traditions. Daniels’s approach also resonated with Fine Dining Lovers insiders, who selected her for their award that honors “a chef’s expression of personal belief.”.

With only minutes to spare, chef Nicolas Lopez of 888 in Nashville arrived with “Pozole or Chawanmushi…?” Combining pozole, corn, and langoustine, Lopez connected his upbringing in Mexico with a culinary journey that has been shaped by Scandinavian ingredients and Japanese techniques. Although the judges could have used more time to explore the dish, they were intrigued by his influences and impressed by his technique.

The final competitor, Juwon Lee, is the chef of Octavia in San Francisco. Lee was born in South Korea and grew up in Singapore before making California his home. His dish, “Curry and Quail with Ingredients My Mother Said Were Healthy,” drew on memories of eating Indonesian fried chicken and his mother’s insistence on including vegetables at family dinners. “I believe in the term happy food,” Lee explained. “There are no restrictions other than bringing joy to the eater and the chef.”.

Industry observers note that congratulations to all 10 chefs who competed, and best of luck to Chef Cacciato as she continues to work with her mentor and prepares to represent the United States at the 2027 Grand Finale in Milan. Follow her journey at @sanpellegrino_us.

5 Restaurant Chains With Troubling Food Safety Records

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (889 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that not every day can be a home-cooked meal kind of day.
  • In a recent development, admittedly, fast food chains don’t always have the best reputation, especially when it comes to health concerns.
  • In a recent development, cleaning protocols differ from chain to chain—and even from location to location.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that not every day can be a home-cooked meal kind of day. Sometimes, going out really pays off. It saves you time in the kitchen, cuts down on effort, and most importantly, lets you relax while someone else does the heavy lifting. Many families turn to fast food when they want an easy, quick meal or when time is of the essence. But where you go can really make a difference.

In a recent development, admittedly, fast food chains don’t always have the best reputation, especially when it comes to health concerns. But beyond the macros, another factor to consider is cleanliness.

In a recent development, cleaning protocols differ from chain to chain—and even from location to location. You may have seen headlines concerning less-than-stellar hygiene reports stemming from certain fast food locations over the years. Kitchen cleanliness is paramount to food safety (just look at this year’s Cyclospora outbreak), and some chains have faced more than their share of troubling headlines. Here are five fast food chains with a disappointing history of food safety issues.

In a recent development, I hate to break it to burrito-with-extra-guac fans, but Chipotle has a history of high-profile food safety complications. The firm paid $25 million to resolve criminal charges related to a series of foodborne illness outbreaks between 2015 and 2018. According to the documents, Chipotle was charged with "adulterating food in violation of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act," resulting in the largest criminal fine ever imposed in a food safety case at the time.

Records cited at least five foodborne illness outbreaks across several states, including incidents involving norovirus, that sickened more than 1,100 people. These outbreaks "primarily stemmed from store-level employees' failure to follow company food safety protocols." Personally, I'd rather have a side of hot sauce than a side of stomach flu.

In February 2025, a Massachusetts store was cited for nine core health code violations—including insufficiently cleaned ice machines, improperly stored produce, and missing thermometers in a walk-in cooler—along with one priority foundation violation. Such issues can raise concerns about food safety and sanitation.

According to recent reports, in 2022, a health inspector described another location in the state as "very unclean." A year before that, workers at a Springfield, Missouri, location staged a walkout over poor working conditions. A subsequent health inspection found that "the floors in the food preparation area (especially under equipment and near drains), walk-in refrigerator and freezer, and dry storage areas were not clean," leading to a follow-up inspection. (Don't even get us started on some of the issues found overseas!).

Sorry, chalupa lovers. Taco Bell has also faced its share of food safety concerns over the years. Reports include an E. coli outbreak along the East Coast in 2006 resulting in 71 illnesses (53 of whom were hospitalized), two Salmonella outbreaks in 2010 affecting at least 155 people across 21 states, and a hepatitis A outbreak in 2000 that sickened 23 people and hospitalized 15.

Recent findings suggest that more recently, a customer’s viral video appeared to show a Taco Bell kitchen strewn with food, garbage, and old boxes near food prep areas. Some commenters suggested that it was filmed during rush hour while the restaurant was understaffed and that employees were too busy to clean. Still, it's not a great look for in-store hygiene.

It has been revealed that significant Mac lovers, look away. The Golden Arches have faced numerous lawsuits over food safety issues over the years, including a class action suit (plus several personal injury suits) filed in 2024 following a multistate E. coli outbreak linked to Quarter Pounders. The outbreak ultimately sickened 104 people and killed one, with investigators identifying slivered onions as the likely source of contamination.

Industry observers note that the Boston City Department of Inspectional Services found nearly 125 violations at seven different McDonald's locations between 2018 and 2019—everything from mismanaged storage to mold, rat droppings, and even live cockroaches. Complaints and lawsuits have also alleged undercooked meat and foodborne illnesses caused by cross-contamination.

Wendy's locations have racked up numerous health code violations, too (one Las Vegas restaurant in particular drew 27 demerits in a 2019 inspection for dirty soda nozzles, food left on the floor, raw food cross-contamination, and more). A 2023 "Dirty Dining" segment called out a Fort Lauderdale, Florida, location with an inspection that found insects all over the restaurant.

According to recent reports, perhaps most concerningly, a Michigan family filed a lawsuit in 2024 alleging their daughter developed hemolytic uremic syndrome following an E. coli infection they attributed to food from Wendy's. According to the lawsuit, the illness caused permanent brain damage, kidney failure, a seizure disorder, and other lasting health problems. Inspectors had found the location in violation of 17 different health and food codes just days before the family's visit, including moldy food, spoiled produce, dirty surfaces, and water leaks.

Industry observers note that even with these histories of violations, not every location should make you rethink your dining options—many restaurants are up to code and clean. While all this information is enough to convince me to stick to home-cooked meals for the rest of my life, I suggest checking your local restaurant's latest health inspection report before deciding whether or not to visit your chain of choice.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that I can happily spend an entire afternoon making dinner.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

"Store-bought is fine" carries a little more weight when Ina tells you exactly which pasta sauce to buy.

Recent findings suggest that I can happily spend an entire afternoon making dinner. Give me a little music, a glass of wine and something to braise, and I’ll settle in without much concern for when it all reaches the table. It’s a lovely way to cook when I have the time, but leisurely cooking isn’t always practical for busy parents. On most days, dinner needs to fit into my family’s schedule, and my kids don’t want to hear that dinner is still achieving key levels of depth and complexity as it enters its sixth hour on the stove.

But having less time to cook shouldn’t lower our expectations for dinner. A simple plate of pasta can be every bit as satisfying—provided the ingredients involved are worth eating. It’s why I’m particular about store-bought sauce. I’m happy to buy it, but I want to enjoy it as much as anything I spent time making myself.

Sources indicate that ina Garten seems to have arrived at a similar conclusion. Her signature “store-bought is fine” reassurance comes with some excellent recommendations, including the marinara from Rao’s Homemade, a brand I’ve been loyal to for years. It’s a small thing to have in common with Ina, but until I acquire a Parisian apartment of my own, I’ll gladly take it.

“Why make your own marinara when Rao’s marinara sauce tastes homemade?” Ina has stated. It’s a reasonable question, particularly coming from someone with very little left to prove in the kitchen.

She’s equally decisive on her website. When a reader asked her favorite jarred marinara, Ina answered, “That’s easy! Rao’s Marinara Sauce.” It also appears among her recommended ingredients in the site’s shopping section.

It has been revealed that her advice to an incoming college student gives the recommendation some practical context. When asked which staples to have on hand, Ina suggested keeping pasta and Rao’s marinara around for a ten-minute dinner. That’s useful advice at any age, particularly once you discover that graduation doesn’t necessarily leave you with more time to cook.

Industry observers note that ina’s comment about homemade flavor gets at why I’ve continued to buy it, too: Rao’s has the richness and depth I want in a sauce, even when I’m serving it with nothing more elaborate than bucatini and Parmesan. I actually look forward to that dinner. The fact that it comes together quickly is just a bonus.

Recent findings suggest that lately, I’ve been especially impressed with the brand’s newly introduced creamy roasted garlic sauce (so much so that I gave it a Taste of Home Award). The mellow roasted garlic and the richness of mascarpone have made it a favorite in my house.

According to recent reports, ina’s explanation of “good ingredients” offers a useful starting point. In Modern Comfort Food, she writes, “They don’t have to be expensive, but they need to be chosen thoughtfully.” Her emphasis is on flavor and choosing ingredients because of what they contribute to the finished dish.

When it comes to Rao’s, she points to slow simmering and good tomatoes, basil, garlic and oregano. That makes the ingredient label a sensible place to begin when comparing jars. The marinara label lists whole peeled Italian tomatoes, followed by olive oil, onions, salt, garlic, basil, black pepper and oregano—and no added sugar.

In a recent development, for a classic marinara, look for that familiar foundation of tomatoes, oil, aromatics and herbs. If you prefer a more savory sauce, keep your eye on the added sugar, too. These are useful details to compare across brands, although the label can only tell you so much about how well the ingredients have been cooked and balanced. In this case, I’m happy to let Ina’s recommendation settle the matter.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

According to recent reports, place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

Sources indicate that do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

While the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

Sources indicate that reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.

BA's Best Orecchiette With Sausage and Broccoli Rabe

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (513 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero.
  • Industry observers note that while orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work.
  • This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero. You can make it start to finish, in about 30 minutes. The key to successful execution is to go way beyond blanching when it comes to precooking the broccoli rabe in boiling salted water. For tender rabe that melds seamlessly with pasta and sausage, start by separating the thick stems from the rest of the stalks and giving them a head start before adding the rest. It removes any unpleasant bitterness and also means the rabe will cook into the saucy base of browned sausage and sweated garlic in just minutes.

Industry observers note that while orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work. Sausage has become a popular addition to the true original Pugliese dish of stewed broccoli rabe with pasta, but a tin of anchovies makes a great substitute for added oomph and intensity.

This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.

Cut 2 large bunches broccoli rabe, trimmed, in half crosswise to separate thick stalks from thinner stems and florets. Cook thicker stalks in a medium pot of boiling salted water until crisp-tender, about 5 minutes. Add thinner stems and florets and cook until all of the broccoli rabe is tender (the tip of a paring knife should slide through the stalks with little to no resistance), about 3 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet with tongs; let sit until cool enough to handle (no need to squeeze out excess water unless dripping wet). Coarsely chop into bite-size pieces.

Meanwhile, cook 1 lb. orecchiette (little ear-shaped pasta) or other short pasta in a second medium pot of boiling salted water until al dente (or use same pot with fresh salted water). Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Sources indicate that heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 1 lb. hot Italian sausage, casings removed if needed, breaking up with a wooden spoon, until golden brown and nearly cooked through, about 5 minutes. Add 1 head of garlic, cloves separated, peeled, thinly sliced, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, breaking up sausage even finer if needed and stirring often, until garlic is golden brown and softened, 3–4 minutes. Add broccoli rabe and cook, stirring occasionally, until very tender and wilted, about 5 minutes.

Add 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter, cut into pieces, pasta, and 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Cook, stirring often and adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is coated in a clingy sauce. Taste and add some crushed red pepper flakes if desired. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup), and stir, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep sauce smooth and shiny, until incorporated; season with salt.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opening a pizza box can bring out the critic in anyone.
  • The chain has introduced a two-week promotion called "Snap a Pizza, Get a Free Pizza," inviting customers to snap a photo of their orders and tell the company what they really think.
  • Before you start snapping pictures of every slice in sight, though, there's some fine print worth reading.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opening a pizza box can bring out the critic in anyone. But whatever your reaction, whether it's about a pale crust or toppings piled onto one side, Papa Johns wants to hear about it—and your opinion could be worth a whole other pizza.

The chain has introduced a two-week promotion called "Snap a Pizza, Get a Free Pizza," inviting customers to snap a photo of their orders and tell the company what they really think. You can praise it, complain about it, or land somewhere in the middle. Even a less-than-glowing review is welcome.

Before you start snapping pictures of every slice in sight, though, there's some fine print worth reading.

To participate, you'll need to spend at least $15 on an order placed through the Papa Johns website or app. You'll also need a Papa Rewards account with text messages enabled, since that's how the chain will contact you about submitting your review.

Papa Johns wants an unedited photo of your pizza, along with your thoughts on everything from the level of cheese and how it's cooked to the overall experience. Once the photo is approved, you'll receive an offer for a large one-topping pizza in your Rewards account.

That word "free" does come with a qualification. Redeeming your reward requires spending at least $5 on your next order, meaning you'll have to open your wallet twice. Still, if you've ever had strong opinions about the way your pizza arrived, you might as well get something out of sharing them.

Of course, Papa Johns is getting something out of this arrangement, too. All those pictures and reviews give the chain a closer look at what customers are actually receiving.

"We see the pizza pics, the unboxings and the hot takes online every day, and we know our customers aren't shy about sharing what they think," noted Chris Lyn-Sue, Papa Johns' global chief marketing officer, in a statement.The promotion is part of Papa Johns' recently unveiled "Unbox Better" initiative, which focuses on things like food quality and the chain’s general service. It's also not the only fast food chain inviting customers to speak their minds. Earlier this year, Burger King went so far as to encourage customers to call or text its president directly with their feedback.

Papa Johns is offering a slightly different incentive, although I suspect a free pizza might convince a few more people to participate.

Sources indicate that available every two, four, eight weeks or twelve weeks, you can choose how often your special, curated box of meat is delivered. And if you’d rather create your own custom subscription box to gift, you can do that too for a gift he’s sure to love.

Men like meat, right? If you’re looking for yet another meat subscription option, this one is bacon specific. Tester Marisa Hillman tried three months of Goldbelly’s bacon club, which offers approximately 2 to 5 pounds of bacon from a newly introduced butcher each month. Her first box, which was her favorite, came with four 14-ounce packages of bacon from The Loveless Cafe in Nashville: hickory, applewood, maplewood and peppered.

“I cooked a package of the Goldbelly bacon, immediately followed by a package of grocery store (Jimmy Dean brand) bacon,” states Marisa. “The difference was incredible. The Goldbelly bacon slices were thick and flavorful with minimal grease left behind. The grocery store bacon slices were thin and I had to empty the grease three times while cooking.”.

Marisa’s second delivery was a bit more adventurous. It included two 12-ounce packages of bacon, one 8-ounce package of jowl bacon and one 8-ounce package of bacon bits from Smoking Goose in Indiana. While she didn’t love the jowl bacon, she did enjoy the bacon bits and Smoking Goose bacon.

Sources indicate that her third box included two 1-pound packages of regular bacon from Benton’s Smoky Mountain Country Hams. Marisa noted that the final shipment contained bacon which was mostly fat. While the fatty cuts didn’t particularly appeal to her, it may to folks who are open to non-traditional bacon—especially adventurous cuts.

Sources indicate that with Murray’s Mac and Cheese Club, he can have fresh warm and gooey macaroni and cheese whenever. The mac and cheese arrives ready to be heated in the oven or stashed in the freezer, so a comforting meal is just moments away when the craving strikes.

Sources indicate that you can opt for a three, six or twelve month subsctiption, and each month brings a shipment of two 32-ounce frozen mac and cheese portions. One is always Murray’s famous, classic cheddar flavor. The other is a different flavor each month that’s exclusive to the club.

According to recent reports, “I received both a regular and spinach and artichoke mac. The mac and cheese looked good right out of the box, and both were still nicely chilled from the ice,” says tester Caroline Lubinsky. “I was a little surprised to see that they were a bit smaller than I expected for the price, but they looked appetizing in the pans.”.

Recent findings suggest that in comparison to other easy, cheesy brands (think Kraft or Annie’s), Murray’s definitely takes the cake. We also like that you receive a specialty flavor each month. While the packaging is more practical than it is pretty, this delicious subscription makes a great gift for someone who loves carbs.

In a recent development, gourmet jerky delivered right to your door? Say less. If you have a jerky lover in your life, this is the gift for them.

Our own resident jerky lover Paul Rankin tried Jerky Dynasty Club and was impressed by everything from the presentation to the products. “I loved how much variety there was in the box, definitely plenty of jerky to get me through an entire month (or more),” he states in this Dynasty Club review.

It has been revealed that paul’s box contained three major bags of jerky and some smaller meat sticks. While the contents were mostly beef and pork jerky, there were also some unexpected meats like venison, elk and wild boar. In total, he received bags of Carnivore Candy Peppered Brisket jerky, Ayoba-yo Droëwors beef sticks, Smoking Gun Wicked Mary jerky and Hunters Reserve Roadkill summer sausage. He also enjoyed an Indian Valley Venison Pepper jerky stick and a Dill Pickle jerky stick. “The flavors were intense and interesting,” says Paul.

According to recent reports, in addition to delicious jerky, Paul points out that this subscription is a great value. “Considering how much a regular bag of jerky is at the grocery store, this subscription box is a great deal,” notes Paul. “A regular bag of jerky is around $12 at my grocery store (for under 3 ounces), and this box gives you 16-24 ounces, so your dollar is really stretching far.”.

The City Brew Tours club really is a club, complete with its own monthly podcast for die-hard brewski fans, making it the perfect subscription gift for hop heads.

According to recent reports, the City Brew Tours staff curates each selection and includes a detailed printout containing information about the tasting notes and breweries chosen, plus a little about the featured city. Inclusions range from sours to IPAs and everything in between, so it’s an ideal subscription for those who appreciate beers of all kinds.

“My box arrived filled to the brim with brews from Pittsburgh. The insert with an overview of the city, facts about Pittsburgh brewing and info about each beer was incredibly enlightening and a great introduction to what the city offers,” states Shopping Editor Emily Way. “It was also cool to have access to the tasting notes and enjoy two brews from each brewery—not to mention all the one-on-one insight gleaned from the Zoom call.”.

In a recent development, you don’t have to know the ins and outs of his home coffee setup to gift this coffee membership subscription. The Cometeer coffee subscription features the convenience of instant coffee without the taste of instant coffee. Score! These genius recyclable capsules rely on flash-frozen coffee concentrate and ship directly to your door.

“I tried several types of Cometeer coffee a while ago, and I’ve been thinking about it ever since. I can’t get over the convenience factor,” indicates Deputy Editor Katie Bandurski. “The pods are perfect on busy (or, let’s be honest, lazy) mornings when I don’t want to pull out my grinder and make a mess of grounds all over the countertop.”.

Recent findings suggest that simply grab a pod from the freezer, mix it with hot water or milk and enjoy it as hot coffee, an iced latte or even an espresso martini. No brewing required! Moreover, Cometeer offers multiple roast options from over a dozen roasters.

And don’t forget to check out the Cometeer Advent Calendar this year as an early Christmas gift for java lovers!

In a recent development, if he likes to indulge in a little charcuterie every now and then, a cheese of the month club is a cool way to shake up the usual cheddar or brie boards. Of all the options we’ve tried, Murray’s reigns supreme for its cheese of the month club. Rather, its cheese of the month clubs. Our favorite is the Cheese Explorer’s Club, which contains three different cheeses from a variety of cheesemakers across the globe each month.

We love the brand’s bold, outside-the-box cheeses from domestic and global cheesemakers, and the fun facts and serving tips included in each box.

Industry observers note that “I got three herby Vermont Creamery Goat Cheeses in the first box of the month. The second month’s box had more variety: Murray’s Gemma Di Langa, Meredith Dairy Sheep and Goat Cheese and Alisios,” notes tester Caroline of her three-month subscription. Even more notably, each box arrived completely chilled.

And surely, you can’t go wrong gifting a snack club. Whether it’s savory or sweet, a box full of delicious treats is a surefire way to show your favorite foodie you care. Universal Yums is our favorite snack subscription that allows you to experience popular snacks from different countries.

Recent findings suggest that in addition tasty treats, each snack delivery box also includes an illustrated map, a tasting worksheet, allergy labels and a pamphlet full of cultural facts, fun quizzes and background info on each treat. The snacks in this international snack box are genuinely sourced from their featured countries, which adds to the authenticity.

“I received the Yum Yum Belgium Box with 10 snacks,” notes product tester Annamarie Higley. “Unpacking this box made me want to pack my bags and head back to Belgium. The snacks were so authentic—every one of them was made within the country’s borders, excluding the chips, and this fact was very prominently noted.”.

Universal Yums is a fun way to explore different cultures through snacks. With three box sizes to choose from, each package includes 5 to 18 snacks. You can choose a one-year subscription, pay for six months, or purchase one month at a time. To get started, pick from about 10 different destinations for your first box and enjoy a taste of somewhere upcoming.

It has been revealed that if you want to give the gift of snacks with a healthier twist, the monthly HealthyMe Living Snack Box is a great option. Each box includes 8 to 10 snacks carefully curated by a certified holistic health coach. Even better, the snacks feature minimal, high-quality ingredients without unnecessary fillers or artificial sweeteners.

Recent findings suggest that the box arrived packed with 10 snacks wrapped in blue tissue paper, and all but one were upcoming to registered dietitian and product tester Nancy Snyder. “From protein bars and popcorn to infused almonds and ginger chews, I was pleasantly surprised by the quality and taste of each snack. I loved the variety and getting to try treats I couldn’t find at my local grocery store,” she notes.

Prefer a specific diet? Choose a vegetarian or gluten-free box. Nancy found that the regular box also offers a nice mix of snacks to suit different dietary preferences.

This one is definitely an acquired taste, but seafood lovers and fans of trendy tinned fish will appreciate the Tinned Fish Club. Each month, members receive two to four premium tins of seafood, plus seasonings and pairing suggestions.

Recent findings suggest that tester Emily was impressed with the packaging and the flavors. “If you love fish and flavor, you really can’t go wrong with this box, which pairs uncommon, flavorful tinned seafood with mouthwatering seasonings, all shipped directly to your door,” she notes.

Each box also includes a brochure with tasting notes, product details and pairing ideas, making it fun to discover something new. “As a big-time tuna fan, I loved receiving a tin of Santa Caterina tuna in Molho Cru sauce, along with mayo, crushed red pepper and pink sea salt to enjoy alongside,” Emily says.

For anyone who loves sardines, mussels, tuna and other seafood specialties, this subscription is a real catch!

Recent findings suggest that to find the best subscription boxes for men, we considered our own extensive testing with gift clubs. Over the course of testing for other lists, we compiled our “best overall” picks to inform this piece. Our expert team of editors and product testers thoroughly tested and evaluated each option in our own homes and kitchens, and we took notes on the following aspects:.

Andy Baraghani's Ditto Café Is His Most Personal Project Yet

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that andy Baraghani is more afraid of becoming stagnant than he is of dying.
  • Recent findings suggest that it is late morning on the first actually chilly day of autumn and we are staring one another down across a stainless-steel prep table, which has been dragooned into use as an island in his outrageously good-looking kitchen.
  • Quite literally in motion since I arrived, Baraghani finishes his point on stagnancy: He fears a life in which he is not learning, moving, or evolving “as a writer, a cook, and a good gay,” he states.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that andy Baraghani is more afraid of becoming stagnant than he is of dying. Stagnancy, he’s quick to clarify, is different from stillness. Stagnancy is like a fetid pond; stillness is meditative. Baraghani seems to be at risk of neither.

Recent findings suggest that it is late morning on the first actually chilly day of autumn and we are staring one another down across a stainless-steel prep table, which has been dragooned into use as an island in his outrageously good-looking kitchen. He is about to make me scones—salty-sweet ones with dates and lemon zest, an offering under development for his forthcoming café Ditto. But first, we’ll need to pop out for cream.

Quite literally in motion since I arrived, Baraghani finishes his point on stagnancy: He fears a life in which he is not learning, moving, or evolving “as a writer, a cook, and a good gay,” he states.

He lives just a few blocks from the Union Square Greenmarket, where niche pepper varieties are at the moment splayed in colorful fractals across folding tables. We have just completed a ground floor tour of the apartment that the chef-cum-writer-cum-chef shares with his husband, Keith Pollock. Now he moves across the kitchen and pauses at the Crittall-style window. It gives me 30 seconds to take inventory of his countertop alliums.

These details feel notable. Baraghani has become a sort of standard-bearer for exquisite seasonal produce and the exquisite life one can lead preparing such stuff. I clock a couple of shallots, which sit in a Swid Powell bowl beside five heirloom tomatoes. It occurs to me that even onions are more beautiful in Baraghani’s universe.

According to recent reports, “Oh,” he says casually, following my gaze. “Torpedo shallots.” As if all of our countertops look like this.

In the decade or so since he became a household name for a certain set of a certain era (food-obsessed aesthetes who love an acidic drizzle and a hard, salty cheese), as a video star for a certain magazine—okay, this one—his fandom has only continued to explode.

His debut cookbook, The Cook You Want to Be, was a New York Times bestseller and the recipient of a James Beard Award. He has more than 370,000 followers across Instagram and TikTok. He’s been called “the Internet boyfriend of our dreams.” Vogue covered his wedding. The New York Times published his ideal Thanksgiving menu. In the last 24 hours alone, Baraghani has been busy beating out creative director Terrence O’Connor for a Best Body prize at the podcast How Long Gone’s inaugural “Goneies” Award Show, (Baraghani was asked to remove his blazer to reveal a formfitting Dario Vitale–era Versace pink tank top) before running into David Tanis while shopping for groceries.

When Baraghani announced he would be opening a restaurant this fall near Union Square with restaurateur Michael Silber, publications began tripping over themselves to cover the news. Still, he indicates, few have pushed him on the true meaning of the name Ditto. Perhaps they were too busy trying to keep up.

In a recent development, baraghani takes a seat on one of the iron stools beside the prep table and there is a rare, brief silence, which is broken almost immediately by the tinny opening notes of a techno song emanating from the crew performing a renovation on the lower floor. I inquire about his cortisol levels as he juggles opening Ditto a few blocks away, the second cookbook he has just shot in this apartment, and now the remodel below us.

Recent findings suggest that baraghani grins. “I feel calm,” he insists. “If something goes wrong, I can fix it, because I feel pretty clear on what I want to achieve.”.

He has spent the last 10 years peppering his recipes with caveats. “I know that my food may be a touch too lemony for some,” he writes in The Cook You Want To Be. “And that I use what has been called a ridiculous amount of herbs.”.

His background too. Years ago, he penned an essay for this magazine about growing up Iranian in a post-9/11 America; he started to go by Andy instead of Andisheh and bought an “Italian Stallion” T-shirt. He wrote about learning to accept his sexuality in restaurant kitchens, where he rarely encountered other gay men, and in his family life. He grew up in the Bay Area, the son of parents who had emigrated from Iran to Berkeley in 1977. The piece ended with an admission: “So as nice as it would be for this story to end with that Iran feature or getting my dream job at Bon Appétit, the truth is that I’m still trying to figure things out. It’s not always steady progress.”.

Recent findings suggest that since I had a baby six weeks ago, I have been walking around floored that the adults in my life could have ever been children, but with Andy, I don’t have to work too hard to picture it. He has a particularly cheerful sense of wonder. When I ask about it, he notes it comes from his upbringing. His parents were political activists. Andy’s mother worked as an aesthetician (yes, he established his famous skin-care routine early). He grew up surrounded by a diverse community of immigrants who would invite his family to their celebrations and into their homes, where a young Baraghani got to taste dishes from far-flung places. After he landed in New York, he would take respite in stints abroad, traveling from hostel to hostel so he could eat his way across Vietnam, Lebanon, and Turkey.

Now, though, Baraghani states he is done footnoting his vision. In the intervening years since that essay, Baraghani has written and cooked and tasted at warp speed. He was bound to self-actualize in the same timeframe it took the rest of us to figure out how to style barrel-leg pants. Or perhaps it’s the reality of having to reckon with what he can’t change: In 2024, after a battle with small-cell lung cancer, his beloved father passed away. Baraghani tells me that before it was stagnancy, his greatest fear was losing a parent. He has since learned that loss isn’t something to solve, but a tremendous void one must learn to live with.

“There’s an explicit confidence you’ll see [at Ditto,]” he says. The dishes will weave together all of the threads of Baraghani-ism: seasonal vegetables prepared deftly with Persian flourishes, blending tart and sour and aromatic with a firm point-of-view. If the specifics seem hard to picture, I think that might be the point. Baraghani has thrived historically by taking a straightforward-seeming dish and twisting it just off-kilter, so it is a few degrees punchier and much more beautiful than you were expecting. The result is food that is as much about the people and places evoked by the flavors as it is about aesthetic provocation. (That Italian Stallion shirt, he tells me, is long gone.).

Sources indicate that literally speaking, Ditto will be a revival of the sort of counter-service restaurant Baraghani has long adored, from Gjusta in Los Angeles to City Bakery in Newly introduced York. He and Silber sprang for a shiny rotisserie oven, for what they’re calling a “beyond chicken program,” with plans for spit-roasted porchetta, romanesco, and cabbage.

The goal is dishes that are palpably human, in a space Baraghani hopes will seem accessible to everyone. It was important for both owners to find a space in a hub neighborhood. With the storefront they chose, a former Agnès B. on 16th Street, Greenmarket shoppers can stop by for a selection of California-ish sides and salads displayed Yotam Ottolenghi–style, counter pastries, or just to peruse marketplace provisions: tahini, harissa, dates (and, for now, no tinned fish). Maybe, one day, they’ll stay open for dinner service, but for now the initiative is breakfast and lunch.

Suddenly Baraghani is moving again, reaching for his phone to show me a photo of a dish he would have loved to serve, had Con Ed turned on the gas in time for a September opening: a mound of spicy tuna salad piled perkily in a blanched tomato with a turret of scallion greens.

The sight makes me hungry, and I realize we still haven’t gone out for that cream. Ninety minutes have passed and I have yet to ask any of the questions I’d prepared for Baraghani, who keeps surprising me with disclosures. (Such as: He did not speak until he was three years old.).

Suddenly, it is time to head to Ditto for a tour, cream and scones be damned.

As we walk over, I ask about the restaurant’s name. He asks if I’ve seen the movie Ghost. I have, but not for a while. “It’s another way to say ‘I love you,’” he indicates simply, before disappearing to join a meeting.

Later I dig up that scene Baraghani mentioned and press play. In it, Whoopi Goldberg tries to convince a frustrated Demi Moore that her recently deceased boyfriend has returned as a ghost. Moore jumps up in disbelief to flee the restaurant as Patrick Swayze, the boyfriend, scrambles to find a way to prove to her that he’s right there. “Tell her ‘ditto,’” he urges Goldberg, who screams “ditto” after Moore as she bolts. “Ditto!” It’s their code word for “I love you too.”.

Moore stops in her tracks and turns, her gaze connecting with a man she misses, who she isn’t totally sure is there.

Recent findings suggest that and for the first time in a while, she is no longer in motion. She is still.

#19564. Tech Report: Is It Safe to Eat Raw Cranberries?

Tech Report: Is It Safe to Eat Raw Cranberries?

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (617 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This holiday star rarely turns up in the fruit bowl.
  • Most of us have likely eaten cranberries without ever trying one on its own.
  • I live near Bandon, the Cranberry Capital of Oregon, where enthusiasm for the fruit extends well beyond Thanksgiving.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

This holiday star rarely turns up in the fruit bowl. Could you eat cranberries raw if you wanted to?

Most of us have likely eaten cranberries without ever trying one on its own. The fruit is familiar enough to be indispensable at Thanksgiving, but rarely considered when we’re in the mood for a bowl of berries to snack on.

I live near Bandon, the Cranberry Capital of Oregon, where enthusiasm for the fruit extends well beyond Thanksgiving. Cranberry bogs are part of the landscape, and local berries fill jars of jam and syrup at roadside stands. This fall, my family attended the annual cranberry festival, where a friend of ours was crowned Cranberry Queen. (It’s a small town.).

In a recent development, even here, though, cranberries generally arrive at the table with enough sugar to soften their bite. That sharpness is welcome in a buttery loaf or in a cranberry sauce alongside a rich turkey dinner, but a plain berry is a very different experience. So is all that preparation a matter of preference, or do cranberries actually need to be cooked before you eat them?

Photography by Paula Thomas/getty Images.

Industry observers note that yes, cranberries are safe to eat raw. There’s no need to cook them first; simply rinse them under cool running water and discard any that are soft, shriveled or spoiled. What happens after that is largely between you and your tolerance for sour foods.

Industry observers note that raw cranberries are firm and sharply tart, with a bitterness that can get lost beneath the sugar in cranberry sauce and muffins. They’re also astringent, meaning they leave you with a dry, puckering feeling in your mouth. If you loved the sour fruit trend of adding citric acid to grapes, then you might happily eat a few plain cranberries, but their absence from the average person’s fruit salad is understandable.

In a recent development, they have plenty to offer nutritionally, too. One cup of raw cranberries provides about 4 grams of fiber and 13 milligrams of vitamin C, along with naturally occurring antioxidants. They’re also naturally low in sugar, though that tends to change once we start mixing them with the things that make us love them.

According to recent reports, I like cranberries best when their tartness is balanced by something rich or sweet. In a cranberry orange bread, the berries become little pockets of sharp fruit that break up the sweetness, while orange zest and warm spices round out the flavor. They do the same for muffins, cakes and scones, where an acid bite is particularly welcome among all that butter and sugar.

It has been revealed that of course, making sauce remains a very good use for a bag of cranberries. Simmering softens the berries until they burst, and sweetening lets you appreciate their flavor without quite so much puckering. At Thanksgiving, that acidity is part of the appeal: A spoonful brings some relief to a plate largely devoted to gravy, cream and butter. I’m equally happy to see the fruit on the next day’s turkey sandwich along with plenty of mayonnaise.

If you’d rather leave the berries uncooked, chopping them finely makes their intensity easier to distribute throughout a dish. A fresh relish with orange and sugar preserves their crisp texture, while cranberry salsa takes them in a savory direction. You can also blend a small handful into a smoothie with sweeter fruit.

According to recent reports, and if you bought more than you need, cranberries freeze beautifully. Set some aside for baking after the holidays. A cranberry-orange loaf will be just as appreciated when the oven has considerably fewer obligations.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that patrick Schwarzenegger knows a thing or two about a good martini. After three years working with Ketel One and spending time with the family behind the vodka, the White Lotus actor has learned that some people take their cocktails very seriously.

Recent findings suggest that "I'm not that severe," Schwarzenegger told me, although he's developed a few preferences of his own. His biggest? "A frosted glass. A cold glass I think makes all the difference.".

I caught up with Schwarzenegger in Schiedam, Netherlands, during a Ketel One-hosted visit to the historic Nolet Distillery, where the family has been making spirits since 1691. The trip was actually his idea. After hearing so much about the distillery from the Nolet family, Schwarzenegger wanted to see everything firsthand, even getting his hands dirty by shoveling coal into the distilling equipment.

According to recent reports, according to Schwarzenegger, family members have gotten so particular about their drinks that they'll check where a bar stores its vermouth, olives, and white wine before ordering. If certain ingredients have been sitting out rather than refrigerated, they might opt for a drier martini.

It has been revealed that bob Nolet sees that same attention to detail in the way people order cocktails today. "Today's martini drinkers know what they want," he told Delish, whether that's a classic dry martini, something dirty, or an espresso version.

Of course, that hasn't stopped bartenders from seeing just how far they can stretch the definition of a martini. Schwarzenegger told me he tried The Corner Store’s viral sour cream-and-onion version largely because he'd heard so much about it, something he deemed “really good.”.

Sources indicate that the Tomatini was another story. He appreciated how convincingly it captured tomato flavor, but the novelty only went so far. "I think that I could have that for a few sips, maybe one max, but then I'm tapped out of that," he said.

His more dependable order is an espresso martini, something the Nolets know particularly well. Schwarzenegger revealed that the family even arranged for espresso machines to be sent to his wedding in Idaho, giving guests a way to enjoy his favorite cocktail during the celebration.

Recent findings suggest that for Carl Nolet Jr., the connection goes deeper than a shared appreciation for espresso martinis. "Patrick comes from a family that is equally committed to their craft in the entertainment space," he told Delish. "You can see that commitment through his career and how he brings his legacy into a latest generation.".

Carl also credits Schwarzenegger with offering a younger perspective on cocktail culture, particularly how drinking has become part of the way people socialize, host, and celebrate.

For someone who knows his way around a cocktail, Schwarzenegger doesn't actually drink all that often. Between filming, fitness, and work, he's made a rule to keep alcohol to weekends. He's also taken an interest in the growing demand for better-for-you options, pointing to canned cocktails with less sugar and real fruit juice as examples of how people's drinking habits are changing.

That curiosity extends well beyond the bar. With his involvement in the protein snack organization MOSH, Schwarzenegger has become the kind of person who considers wandering supermarket aisles a perfectly good Friday night activity. One of his first stops after arriving in the Netherlands was a grocery store, and he loves comparing what's available in different places, from Los Angeles to wife Abby Champion's home state of Alabama.

In a recent development, his Instagram algorithm isn't helping matters, either. Food, drinks, random syrups—if an ad catches his attention, there's a decent chance it'll end up on his doorstep. "I buy everything," he admitted.

Interestingly, all that enthusiasm for trying new things doesn't necessarily translate to elaborate dinners. He and Champion love exploring restaurants together, but they're equally happy cooking at home or keeping things simple. She's a fan of Chick-fil-A and In-N-Out, while he's perfectly content with a plate of chicken and rice.

After talking martinis with Schwarzenegger and the Nolets, I might start paying a little more attention to what happens behind the bar. I'll leave the vermouth inspections to the professionals, but keeping the rest of my martini on ice until I'm ready for a fresh, frosty glass? That's a level of service I could get used to.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“I don’t have time” should never be an excuse to skip breakfast. Take this overnight oat–chia pudding hybrid, which comes together in barely 10 minutes. (I’m betting that’s less time than it takes to stand in line at the grocery store to buy a container of worse-tasting, more expensive oatmeal!) Grab a can of pumpkin and some baking staples, mix it up, then pop the bowl in the fridge. The next morning you’ll be rewarded with a lightly sweet, mousse-like treat that’s actually good for you—don’t forget to finish each bowl with a dollop of yogurt for a pumpkin-pie-with-whipped-cream vibe. Self-care rarely tastes this good.

Using an unsweetened soy or nut milk will keep the pudding more pumpkin-forward than dairy milk (and keeps the recipe vegan, of course), but any milk you have on hand will work here.

In a recent development, healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares nourishing, craveable recipes that you can pull off in 10 ingredients or fewer.

20 minutes (plus 8 hours for chilling).

Sources indicate that whisk one 15-oz. can pure pumpkin purée, 1½ cups unsweetened milk of choice, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, ¼ cup pure maple syrup, and ½ tsp. ground cinnamon or cardamom in a large bowl until smooth. Add 3 Tbsp. chia seeds and whisk to combine. Let sit 10 minutes. (Doing this gives the seeds a head start on hydrating and prevents them from sticking together. But if you can’t spare the time, just give the mixture a good stir before serving.).

Stir chia mixture again, then add 1¼ cups old-fashioned oats and mix well to combine. Cover oat mixture and chill at least 8 hours.

Spoon oat mixture into bowls and top with plain whole-milk yogurt, unsalted roasted pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or granola, maple syrup, and cinnamon as desired.

Do Ahead: Oat mixture (without toppings) can be made 4 days ahead. Keep chilled.

In a recent development, this baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal. Classic twice-baked potatoes require two trips to the oven to deliver a pillowy, gussied-up filling and crispy skins all in one bite. Here, I’ve streamlined the workflow with a microwave. By zapping your spuds to start, you can reduce the overall baking time without sacrificing texture. Pick a large russet (or Idaho) for the best results; their relatively high starch and low moisture content helps them bake up airy and light, not gummy.

In a recent development, the rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks. Cream cheese and mozzarella pack in enough dairy richness for a satisfying cheese pull and mellow out the subtle bitterness of baby spinach and nutty tang of artichoke hearts. (It’s vital that your cream cheese is room temperature before you mash it in with the veggies. If it’s still got a chill from the fridge, it won’t fully incorporate.) The Worcestershire sauce is optional, but just a few shakes from the bottle bring instant savory depth to the filling.

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

According to recent reports, preheat oven to 425°. Poke 1 large russet potato (about 12 oz.) all over with a fork; rub with avocado or vegetable oil to coat and sprinkle with kosher salt. Microwave potato on a microwave-proof plate on high 5 minutes. Turn potato over and microwave on high until fork-tender, about 5 minutes more. Let potato sit until just cool enough to handle.

According to recent reports, while potato is cooling, microwave 5 oz. baby spinach with 2 Tbsp. water in a medium microwave-proof glass bowl until wilted, about 2 minutes. Carefully press leaves to release as much liquid as possible, then drain off liquid. Coarsely chop spinach.

Mix 2 Tbsp. cream cheese, room temperature, in a medium bowl until smooth. Add spinach, 4 quartered artichoke hearts (from a 14-oz. can), coarsely chopped, 2 Tbsp. finely grated Parmesan, 2 Tbsp. coarsely grated mozzarella, ½ tsp. garlic powder, and ¼ tsp. Worcestershire sauce (if using) and fold to combine; season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

It has been revealed that slice potato in half lengthwise and lightly fluff flesh in each half. Set on a small foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Divide spinach mixture between potato halves, piling high (don’t pack too tightly). Sprinkle more Parmesan over. Bake potato halves until very tender when squeezed and skin is wrinkled and crisp, 20–25 minutes. Let cool slightly before eating.

Stanley Tucci isn't settling for pretzels and peanuts on his next flight!

It has been revealed that between busy airport security lines and delays, eating while traveling can be unpredictable. And sure, maybe you ate breakfast before leaving the house. But then suddenly it’s six hours later and you’re struggling to navigate your way to baggage claim with a headache and a growling stomach. Trust me, I’ve been there too many times!

Which is why I have one simple rule when traveling: Eat when you can. Packing plenty of plane snacks is important, but getting a full meal is really ideal. So when I saw the kind of food that Stanley Tucci brings on flights, I felt incredibly validated. However, I don’t know if I could manage something quite this messy in the air.

In a recent development, in a very charming TikTok video, Stanley Tucci’s wife Felicity Blunt records him as he unwraps his plane snack. I watched in shock and awe as he unwrapped aluminum foil to reveal a sandwich. But not just any sandwich—I mean, this is Stanley Tucci we’re talking about. He’s known for whipping up Italian meals for pop stars and cooking cozy comfort meals on a whim. It’s no real surprise then that he brought eggplant Parmesan on a plane!

His wife joked that they should “film a before and after” of his shirt. I mean, this sandwich looks incredible. It’s got tons of creamy marinara sauce and is piled high with thinly sliced eggplant and cheese. The bread is toasted and really looks like it’s doing the best job it can at containing the feast within.

Would I have the confidence to eat an eggplant Parmesan sandwich on a plane? Probably not. I am a notoriously messy eater to begin with, and if bibs were more socially acceptable for adults, I would wear one with every meal. So I can’t imagine diving into this on a plane!

But Stanley loves it. In fact, he’s the one who made the sandwich, or “Stan-wich” as Felicity calls them, for the plane ride. So maybe I need to amend my earlier assertion: I would eat eggplant Parmesan on a plane if Stanley Tucci made it for me.

What’s your go-to airplane snack? Is it as messy as this one? Sound off in the comments below!
